We establish the global existence of a unique solution for a class of nonlinear particles with spin-1/2 semilinear equations. For these equations to support a solution globally, the Lochak-Majorana condition must be met; when this condition is violated only slightly, no solution can exist.

This paper details the creation of a deep learning model for identifying histopathologic structures within image patches (500 × 533), utilizing 3,800 training samples and a testing set of 333 structures. Drawing on data from a collaboration across ten European universities specializing in oncology, the study emphasizes data sharing challenges and a university's private pathology archives as an obstacle to constructing generalizable models. To address this, the work integrates principles from federated learning to ensure cross-institutional applicability. Generalization is enhanced by training the model exclusively on images from a single collaborating university—which then serves as part of the private test hold-out set—while leveraging data contributions from all other nine institutions as part of the training hold-out collection. A convolutional neural network with thirteen layers and approximately 140,000 parameters was designed to analyze these image patches. To confirm the model's ability to handle varied institutional data sources, the authors employed a three-pronged evaluation on images from all ten partners: comparing performance benchmarks against a baseline model trained and assessed solely on one institution's data.

Recent advancements in reinforcement learning (RL) offer a promising pathway for accelerating the development of quadrupedal locomotion controllers, yet their practical deployment remains a hurdle because typical RL implementations demand extensive sim-time before yielding usable policies, a process that hinders integration with standard hardware because it takes a long while to develop valid control strategies via reinforcement learning. To address this limitation while making it easier to integrate with hardware within a reasonable hardware deployment timeframe, this paper introduces a new RL-driven solution where an evolutionary trajectory generator creates the environmental paths instead. This hybrid approach significantly accelerates policy learning speed compared to traditional methods and reduces computational latency so that decision making works in real world conditions. Extensive hardware experiments and simulations demonstrate its superiority by producing smoother gaads with greater anti-tipping capabilities than current methods; furthermore, this proposed framework shows clear advantages in generating more efficient movements than previous approaches as demonstrated through comparative testing on robots.

Super-massive black holes (SMBHs), entities ranging from $10^6$ to $10^{10}$ solar masses, are thought to be a standard feature in both distant galaxies and our own Milky Way. While far away, these objects often appear as low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs); they emit significantly less than what is expected from their accretion rates occurring at radiative efficiencies near 1%. This paper investigates the accretion mechanisms responsible for such low luminosity states within galaxies like LLAGNs. Specifically through two-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations incorporating magnetism, magnetic fields are found to facilitate the formation of accretion columns, facilitating simultaneous formation in multiple points across a protoplanetary disk. This development leads to an enlarged inner disk instability zone, helping to explain the under-accreting nature of SMBHs, particularly the ones present within our own galaxy.

Reinforcement learning has recently emerged as a powerful tool for solving control challenges. This paper introduces a novel model-free RL approach specifically designed to redesign controllers for closed-loop systems already stabilized by an existing controller. Unlike standard RL methods that rely on open-loop signals, this technique generates valuable data exclusively through deliberate controller modifications, maintaining the closed-loop nature of the process. Consequently, the need for external signal injectors or the collection of rare historical data is eliminated, making the method highly practical. While standard RL learns value functions for arbitrary states, this RL design learns for states defined by specific controller parameters, enabling the direct learning of the policy gradient. Using this learned gradient allows for offline controller updates that guarantee closed-loop stability regardless of whether a cost function is provided. Simulations demonstrate that this approach successfully achieves performance enhancements of up to 70% without requiring a predefined cost function.

The SiD Tracker represents a key detection system proposed for the International Linear Collider's (ILC) novel detector design. engineered from numerous individual silicon strip sensor modules, it aims to accomplish precise tracking for both electron and gamma interactions across a remarkably wide momentum spectrum, extending up to 50 GeV. By analyzing several tracking concept designs—each featuring distinct silicon module arrangements, front-end readout electronics configurations, and data processing algorithms—the study seeks to refine the SIpner module interface and validate the concept of Fast Front-End Acquisition (SFFA). The latter employs swift data filtering strategies at the hardware or initial processing stage. Several strategies were explored to further evaluate their efficacy within the module framework and to ensure seamless data transfer downstream. Results indicate concept designs offering superior performance achieve better than 1% momentum resolution for high momentum particles ($p^{\ast} = 50$) while maintaining particle identification capabilities with negligible timing uncertainty ($\sigma_t < 0.5$ ps). Additionally, these designs demonstrate robust resilience against high-luminosity particle fluxes expected during $\gamma\gamma$ collisions with beamstrahlung.

Identifying spatio-temporal anomalies in urban datasets is crucial for diverse industries, yet current approaches relying on contrastive or supervised strategies are hindered by the scarcity of labeled data and the labor-intensive nature of manual tagging. Furthermore, these methods often fail to capture the intricate interdependencies characteristic of heterogeneous sources. To address these issues, this study introduces "CityGuard," a novel unsupervised framework designed to automatically detect spatio-temporal anomalies across multi-city infrastructures. CityGuard integrates deep graph neural networks with contrastive self-supervised learning to analyze raw sensor data, effectively modeling complex dependencies among varying data types. Leveraging cities' structural similarities allows the method to employ transfer learning, requiring training only on a single dataset to generalize reliably to others. Validated using authentic data from three distinct urban areas, results demonstrate that CityGuard consistently surpasses existing baselines. Notably, its performance on uncontaminated test sets rivals the accuracy of algorithms that were explicitly fine-tuned with labeled data from specific target environments.

The primary challenge in obtaining high-precision vertical aerosol optical depth ($\tau_v$) via stellar photometry lies in accurately determining the atmospheric transmission coefficient ($T$). Addressing this, a two-frequent stellar photometry strategy combined with a novel approach for deriving $T$ was employed to measure the daily mean $\tau_v$ for four $V$-band stars over a span of 1,81 days at an observatory in Delhi, India. Results indicated that this methodology achieves a determination of $\Delta T \approx 0.002$ with an accuracy of $\approx 0.025$. A critical finding confirmed that the proposed technique for calculating $T$ remains unaffected by the frequency used during observation.

Detecting voiced speech, estimating the fundamental frequency, and identifying phonemes are crucial components underlying various speech technology techniques such as voiced speech detection, pitch tracking, and phoneme recognition. In this study, we present a deep neural network capable of performing voiced speech detection and pitch estimation concurrently. By introducing a new proposed loss function tailored for both binary classification and regression on pitch frequency, we achieve a 3% relative improvement in detection accuracy using the standard F1 score compared to existing methods. Additionally, our approach reduces detection latency by approximately from 13% to near-zero, achieving nearly complete pitch estimation accuracy for the majority of detected frames with only a minimal compromise in overall speed.

We introduce a new Dynamic Weighted Forward-Backward-Over-Step (DWIFOB) algorithm designed to address structured convex composite optimization problems. Its derivation stems from applying the recently developed Dynamic Extrapolated Forward-Backward Split method to a specific diagonal sum of norms representing the given objective. We demonstrate the theoretical validity of this approach with the proven convergence of the resulting dynamic algorithm, demonstrating superior convergence rates relative to widely used reference algorithms like those of Chambolle-Pock. In a specific section, we propose a practical, straightforward implementation strategy for DWIFOB that leverages sparse diagonal operations suitable for use within optimization software packages. We further present two critical practical variants: one tailored for problems involving a single sum component and another for those defined by two sums. The effectiveness and practicality of these algorithms are demonstrated through a comprehensive numerical evaluation on a diverse set of machine learning tasks, including sparse multiclass classification, two-way linking problems, Lasso regression, and sparse composite support vector machine optimization.

This paper operates within a setup featuring six fermion singlets under the SM gauge group, constructed on the fourth cohomology class of the Chiral Zero profile defined on the Non-Commutative Brane (NCBrane). It posits that finite but negligible neutrino masses arise through a mechanism of spontaneous dimensional decompensation, while zero-level masses for other fields remain unchanged. The analysis confirms the stability of SM-like zero-mode fields—comprising four boson components and three fermial components—against corrections arising in the potential and kinetic terms. Furthermore, it demonstrates that both the generated neutrial mass scales down proportionally to the squared dimensional decompensation parameter and the theory scale $\Lambda$. The resulting SM-like sector effectively communicates with external degrees of freedom through dimensions scaling as $N-2$, where $N$ represents the total spacelien number; this interaction yields consistent results that can be compared against experimental data.

Recent years have seen neural architecture search (NAS) emerge as a pivotal method for automatically creating deep learning models. However, current dominant techniques confine themselves to predefined, limited search spaces defined by a fixed set of building blocks and operations, ultimately capping performance based on the quality of these pre-selected components. These methods struggle to generalize beyond their specific domains because their scope is narrowly bounded. Expanding this pre-determined space to introduce more diverse structures inherently lengthens the search time, creating a fundamental scalability conflict between exploration efficiency and potential performance, a challenge previously considered difficult to resolve. This paper introduces Venus: a neural NAS approach optimized for abstract search spaces that successfully mitigates this contradiction. Venus dynamically models a neural architecture as a latent point within a continuous manifold and employs a learned latent distribution to guide the search, effectively balancing exploration and exploitation while accommodating complex, user-defined search spaces. Empirical evaluations across various tasks demonstrate Venus' superiority over existing baselines in both performance and efficiency. Furthermore, the method reliably converges to high-quality designs within custom spaces, confirming its capability to successfully explore abstract design landscapes.

Communication bottlenecks represent a significant obstacle to the widespread adoption of Federated Learning. Recently introduced, Federated Distillation presents an alternative to standard federated training by replacing gradient-based updates with model output prediction sharing. Although promising, initial findings suggest that Distillation suffers from substantial communication inefficiency, as it relies on transmitting high-weight model embeddings for every participating client in each round. We address this limitation by replacing individual client embeddings with aggregated ones, reducing transmission per round to just one aggregated vector. We assess both approaches regarding communication load and training performance. Results indicate that while both methods achieve comparable model performance and training stability, Federated Distillation via aggregation offers significant savings compared to sending individual client data repeatedly. We open-source our implementation at https://github.com/iea-federation-federation.

Named Data Networking (NDN) represents a promising architecture for evolving distributed computing networks, operating by directing data requests to the specific locations where content resides. This report outlines the development of request and response content processing capabilities within NDN. Request handling involves analyzing content names to extract contextual details, while handling the corresponding responses may necessitate data restructuring or transformation. We introduce this processing logic applied to a scenario wherein applications are developed directly within NDN. Furthermore, we have deployed these mechanisms in the NDN emulation platform, NEMO, to measure their impact on network latency.

Recent studies have demonstrated that neural-network-dependent RL agents are vulnerable to adversarially perturbed inputs; however, crafting such inputs is computationally demanding as the search through the high-dimensional input landscape is difficult. We introduce a straightforward generator that produces effective adversarial samples in polynomial time by utilizing the spectral norm of the input feature matrix in conjunction with randomized Gaussian noise. By leveraging the polynomial scalability of the singular value decomposition, our approach maintains efficiency regardless of sample size increases. While primarily suited for attack scenarios, this generator can also be deployed defensively: either by augmenting training datasets with these generated perturbations to bolster robustness, or by refuting false positives that arise from adversaries mimicking legitimate data distributions.

We introduce a robust superconducting order parameter for two-dimensional electronic lattices that tilts with significant magnitude near the Fermi surfaces nested by a charge density wave. This robustness holds regardless of specific interactions defining the charge density wave, unlike most scenarios where the order parameter is small and fragile near these fixed points. By modeling cold atoms in optical potentials—which also generate optical-induced fragile order parameters—we aim to provoke superconductivity via the combined action of a CW electromagnetic wave and a slowly cooled CW electromagnetic field within closely spaced Dirac cones. This cooling strategy induces the transition from a charge density wave state directly to the proposed superconducting phase. Notably, this phase features an unusual gap structure involving in-plane nodes connecting two electron pockets of opposite curvature within the first Brillouin zone, resembling optical analogues previously observed in photonic lattices.

Distributed machine learning (DML) across time-varying networks enables emerging applications like autonomous driving and mobile device sensor processing by allowing collaborative model training with data privacy preserved through the avoidance of centralised information aggregation. Nevertheless, existing methods struggle because standard communication relies on guaranteed delivery, assumes balanced participant workloads, and ignores the impact of packet drops on convergence. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Resilient Event-triggered DML, the first robust approach that delivers guaranteed convergence despite inevitable network packet losses and disparate workloads across nodes. By implementing a decentralized event-triggered mechanism, the system drastically reduces communication frequency while ensuring convergence through the ability of workers to resume training failed tasks locally upon disconnects or drops. Empirical results demonstrate that this resilient method guarantees convergence regardless of network reliability or failed delivery scenarios, achieving up to a 90% reduction in communication events compared to conventional event-triggered systems.

This study introduces an on-chip multi-grating apparatus designed to bridge single atoms and integrated photonics by directing and focusing laser beams into an optical dipole trap for a single Rubidium atom. Additionally, it offers versatile routing options for single photons via different waveguides, which is essential for constructing scalable quantum information systems.

This paper introduces two new two-particle observables specifically designed to isolate the charge-dependent correlations arising from the Chiral Magnetic Effect in heavy-ion collisions, effectively eliminating potential fake signals related to event plane correlations. Additionally, we demonstrate an "inner desert"—a sparse region predicted to exist inside the HZ for planets smaller than 5–10 Earth masses. Our findings remain robust even when accounting for the minimum mass-semi-major axis relation derived via radial velocity surveys and are reinforced by observations that many exoplanets reside near or at the outer edge of the habitable zone.

Biological agents prioritize available information based on relevance, a capability termed "biased sampling" which is vital for artificial agents with limited environmental perception to perform complex tasks. While recent efforts have attempted to instill this behavior into neural networks through evolutionary strategies, these efforts face challenges such as poor sample efficiency and a restricted generalization beyond simple stimuli. In contrast, this paper presents a biologically inspired, reinforcement learning-driven approach coupled with a dedicated neural circuitry that enables agents to consistently focus attention. By integrating a recurrent sampling controller, the system grants the ability to sustain attentional states, decouples task progression from attention mechanisms, and enhances learning efficiency by an order of magnitude, all across diverse problem scenarios.

This work investigates the phase transition between condensed and normal phases of dark matter in the context of a U(1)_{R} symmetric supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model (SUSY-SM). We analyze the vacuum structure using a fermion loop determinant incorporating superpartner contributions alongside perturbation theory for scalar interactions. At tree level in the scalar interaction, we identify two distinct vacuum scenarios in the presence of spontaneous U(1)_{R} symmetry: the unbroken phase and the spontaneously broken phase. Specifically, the condensed phase emerges from the broken phase at the superpartner tree level via a Z2 symmetry. By employing the one-loop fermion determinant in the fermionic sector with U(1)_{R} fermionic charge, we compute the effective potential for scalar potentials and examine how condensed dark matter properties depend on various densities and temperature regimes. We find that the condensed phase persists up to the critical density where it merges with the normal phase in zero-temperature limits. Furthermore, finite temperature analyses reveal phase transitions of both first and second order; at zero density, these transition first. However, at specific fermionic densities beyond which the first-order transition ceases to exist exclusively the second-order transition exists. Our results demonstrate that only second-order phase transitions exist for all densities above certain critical thresholds.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are highly versatile for generating sequential data but often over-fit rapidly due to excessive capacity and become under-utilized because of inefficient resource allocation in computer architecture. We introduce Locality Masked RNNs (LM-RNNs), a method designed to mitigate these issues by restricting recurrent weight propagation to immediate local neighbors within the computational graph. This structural constraint promotes better parameter distribution, enhancing both resource efficiency and computational effectiveness. Experiments reveal that fully-connected RNNs (FC-RNNs) outperform bi-directional LSTM units in RNN architectures, matching or surpassing their performance while requiring fewer parameters, thereby offering equivalent training speed, inference capability, and inference capability (re: parameter count). This advancement also introduces a novel variant of gated RNN (LRNNs), which can learn to dynamically adjust the recurrence topology based on sequence context using computed gates.

Training deep neural networks for semantic segmentation is typically constrained by the high costs associated with labeling imagery. Furthermore, we address the automated generation of template templates an challenge by proposing a method for extracting templates automatically. Building on the prevalence of vast datasets, supervised learning has become a dominant force in autonomous driving research. Nevertheless, the challenge of acquiring extensive labeled datasets limits its applicability in real-world driving scenarios, where annotating data entails prohibitive costs. To overcome this limitation, we introduce "UnDriv," a framework designed for unlabelled driving data that utilizes the information within driving scenes to enhance prediction models without relying on manual labels. Our approach functions by leveraging the abundance of real-scene driving data to identify and refine the features essential for representing driving tasks within specific neural network architectures. Specifically, we introduce an optimization strategy uncoupled from labeled data, one that utilizes an unsupervised loss function anchored in the concept of downstream task clusters to optimize how driving neural networks encode scenes. Our method effectively captures the encoding requirements for multiple, varied driving tasks and demonstrates robust performance across various benchmarks for both perception and planning. Source code can be accessed at https://em3tun.github.io/Undriving/.

Over the past few decades, Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have driven groundbreaking advancements in computer vision, speech recognition, and other significant areas within machine learning. Yet, despite this remarkable success, ANNs face critical hurdles regarding computational efficiency and generalization. Concurrently, recent years have witnessed considerable achievements with Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), offering a biologically plausible solution to these challenges by mimicking neuronal communication through discrete action potentials or "spikes." By leveraging hardware optimized for sparse events activities, SNNs achieve superior computational performance compared to ANN equivalents. This paper introduces a novel methodology utilizing SNNs to enhance both the convergence rate and classification accuracy when classifying images. Specifically targeting the MNIST dataset, we employed fully connected SNNs to demonstrate empirical support for these claims.

The widespread adoption of open scientific datasets combined with freely available volunteer computing platforms enables researchers to perform complex analyses on substantial data without incurring any extra costs. We present an approach to solving nonlinear eigenproblems by approximating the eigenbracket of a function $f(z)$ at nodes $\lambda$ using a rational uniform interpolant $z[z|\lambda_i]_n$ of order $n$. This method utilizes $n+1$ powers and $n+1$ roots of values. We provide a recursive algorithm for generating this rational interpolant and a subsequent deflation technique to resolve distinct roots and their corresponding multiplicities. Using these tools, a iterative scheme iterates to find the solutions and their respective eigenbrackets. We prove the theoretical convergence of this method in the area where $|\bar{z}_i - \lambda|/\bar{z}_i < 1$ and demonstrate its effectiveness through examples, including the inversion of matrices related to Toeplitz structures. The method's success is illustrated using various nonlinear eigenvalue problems.

Machine learning models like Random Forests and Gradient Boosted Trees are widely valued for their performance and transparency, as feature importance metrics can elucidate key drivers behind predictions. However, these metrics offer limited granular insights for individual decisions and often fail to capture the dynamic influence of features across different data contexts. This study introduces "Disentangled Attribution Curves" (DAT), a technique that reveals conditional feature importance dynamically for single decisions. By analyzing and disentangling activations within neural networks trained on tabular data—mimicking the processing logic inherent in tree ensembles—the approach tracks feature contributions holistically. When implemented in a benchmark simulation, it successfully identified dominant drivers of income and salary predictions that traditional importance metrics entirely overlooked. Consequently, DAT serves as a powerful tool for uncovering nuanced drivers of machine learning decisions, exceeding the capabilities of existing methods.

Federated learning enables distributed training of machine learning models by allowing a server to aggregate local updates from clients while preserving data privacy; however, this approach risks exposing sensitive information through communication channels. Emerging solutions utilizing Trusted Execution Environments (TEE) offer enhanced confidentiality by performing updates inside secure enclaves. Despite their security baseline, current TEE-based methods still require transmitting raw data between the server and clients, creating unnecessary communication overhead. We introduce FL-PreShare, a novel TEE-secured architecture for federated learning that privatizes data before transmission. By conducting all interactions within a TEE, we drastically reduce data transfer frequency between server and clients. Our solution implements pre-sharing mechanisms that support multiple sequential updates from the same client, further optimizing efficiency. We evaluated FL-PreShare across several classifiers on three standard datasets and compared it with existing TEE protocols. Results demonstrate a substantially lower update transmission count relative to current approaches, while maintaining comparable model accuracy.

Developing microservices applications necessitates effective system call (syscall) filtering to ensure safety while maximizing application functionality. Existing solutions generally fall short in either safety or usability for this purpose. On the one hand, purely rule-based methods often fail to provide comprehensive coverage, resulting in excessive permission counts that complicate manual refinement. On the other hand, static analysis-based approaches frequently introduce excessive blocked syscalls by failing to account for dynamic execution contexts. We propose "Timeloops," a novel, highly precise technique that achieves fine-grained syscall filtering through dynamic, iteration-sensitive static analysis rather than relying solely on static rules. By leveraging hardware support for timed loops, Timeloops employs context-aware, dynamic, inter-iterational slicing to identify the precise runtime scenarios triggering specific syscalls within loop structures. This capability ensures a higher degree of precision compared to traditional static methods while automatically reducing the volume of reviewed syscalls, thereby significantly lowering manual refinement efforts. Empirical results demonstrate that our method generates fewer than 10% of the syscalls blocked by comparable static analysis systems across various workloads—a substantial improvement over baseline dynamic approaches without compromising safety.

Compressive learning emerges as a low-complexity approach for handling massive data sets by leveraging sparsity and data structure to decrease both memory requirements and algorithmic complexity. Within this context, compressive matrix factorization offers a specific technique for approximating a stored matrix by identifying an implicit factorization that satisfies certain constraints. Recently, the field has seen growing interest in applying random initializations with various graph-based graph matrices that offer sparsity and structured properties. Although these strategies offer flexible ways to customize learning sparsity and complexity based on available resources, current iterative graph matrix factorization methods predominantly follow a random-walk initialization strategy for factor selection—which we identify as a primary source of excessive initial computational overhead. To mitigate this, we introduce novel initializations for factor matrices that exploit both arithmetic-random matrix structure and graph properties. By integrating these advanced techniques with an SVD-based matrix factorization initialization, we substantially lower startup computational costs compared to traditional random approaches across multiple benchmark examples while maintaining high accuracy. Experimental results across synthetic datasets and real-world data confirm that our proposed methods significantly surpass existing compression learning strategies in efficiency.

The daily path of the sun was pivotal for classical Islamic civilisation, as its rise and set points dictated religious rituals, including prayer orientations and fasting during solstices and equinoxes. Before modern astronomy, determining these limits relied on solar observations reported by indigenous observers or inferences drawn from geographical data. Although urban layouts featured mihrabs to indicate prayer direction, general buildings lacked structures to track solar visibility, yet daily and yearly solar cycles remained central to mosque design. This study examines the role of solar cycles in mosque architecture through a comprehensive 3D computational historic solar analysis covering the region from Morocco to Iraq/Iran (2020 AD). Focusing primarily on mosque plan patterns from the seventh to ninth Islamic centuries in Western and Central Asia/West Iran, we developed an extensive dataset comprising over 1,600 mosques. This collection was expanded soon after with more than 100 newly scanned mosques from Morocco and Western Algeria. The expansion included these sites due to their rich early pattern history and distinct Western Algiers solar observation towers known for tracking solar movements over millennia.

Furthermore, numerical simulations validate the analytical findings and demonstrate the versatility of the proposed mechanism across the entire spectrum of operations, from pure EE maximization to pure privacy preservation.

This paper investigates the influence of quantum ingredients on the quasinormal modes of a Kerr black hole. While classical Schwarzschild and Kerr black holes exhibit imaginary quasinormal modes that correspond to damping (negative amplitude), incorporating semi-classical quantum elements reverses this characteristic, resulting in modes with varying signs for both their real and real components of amplitude. These findings imply a black hole stable under quantum conditions or, alternatively, gravitational wave signatures from merging black holes that can be used to explore quasinormal physics.

At low energy scales, electrons within doped graphene sheets are modeled as massless Dirac fermions moving within a two-dimensional space characterized by metric $\eta_{ab}$ ($a,b=0,1$), embedded as a self-gravity-bearing structure into the three-dimensional Minkowski space-time ($c_\mu$, where $\mu=0,1,2,3$). This model treats the electron gas not as uniformly distributed but as undergoing fluctuations in its linear charge density along the surface. Under the assumption of a weak gravitational influence on these Dirac fermions, we calculate the heat capacity of the electron fluid within this framework, specifically examining how terms related to the energy-momentum tensor of the gravitational field influence the low-temperature thermodynamic limits. The analysis particularly explores how electrofluctuations alter the specific heat of the system in the deep quantum regime. The study finds that gravitational terms modify the standard low-temperature $T\ln T$ behavior typically associated with 2D Dirac fermions, while electrofluctuations restore the conventional specific heat trend but modify its coefficient by imposing an effective stiffer equation of state on the metric.

Human conversations consist of non-verbal speech characterized by a static vocal timbre combined with dynamic speech rates and intropic contours determined by the speaker's emotional state. Mastering these features is essential for high-quality paragraph-level speech synthesis. However, existing approaches struggle with this due to two main hurdles: first, modeling continuous rate and contour simultaneously within a continuous flow is inherently difficult; second, learning the joint distribution of these variations alongside the speaker's identity is complex, as their interaction uniquely defines the emotional expression. To address these challenges, we present SPEACT (Speaker Emotional Audio Codec), a novel framework consisting of a speaker-specific emotional encoder, a speaker-independent codec trained with unsupervised data augmentation, and a speaker-specific variational rate-contour model (SRC). Unlike prior segmented methods, SPEACHT generates fluid synthesis through separate control of rate and intonation, while effectively handling the intricate relationship between speaker identity and emotion through its designed architectural components. Extensive testing confirms significant improvements in perceived speech realism across numerous datasets and large-scale unsupervised pre-training demonstrates the model's potential given sufficiently extensive unsupervised corpora.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel in diverse domains, yet they attract vulnerability to adversarial attacks that expose inherent model fragility. Recent studies have identified that perturbations introduced by quantization during hardware deployment functions similarly to adversarial examples, causing unexpected drops in accuracy; this phenomenon is now recognized as a "quantization attack." While previous work primarily examined the relationship between model training and quantization granularity from an attack perspective, this study shifts the focus to post-training system designers. We introduce "QuantumFGSM," a quantity-aware, quantization-specific adversarial attack that generates robust samples by learning an attack perturbation direction effective across multiple denormalization and quantization schemes. Our methodology involves learning a coarse attack in a high-precision model first, then refining it through a backward search within a low-precision model by evaluating prediction shifts at each bit transition. By isolating quantization as the primary driver of the attack, our generators produce highly efficient bits-specific attacks tailored to specific hardware configurations, significantly surpassing standard attack benchmarks by 50% to nearly fivefold in low-bit scenarios. Consequently, our results offer hardware architects critical insights into attack robustness, facilitating the design of more secure and adaptive systems.

A significant challenge in climate communication is the widespread presence of conspiracy theories. Results indicate that climate skeptics are the primary drivers behind messages containing conspiracy-centric keywords, with the spread of these concepts varying across different rumors. Finally, we explore the consequences of these observations for effective climate communication strategies.

Image restoration and image segmentation are two pivotal areas within computer vision that have attracted significant interest. While researchers have previously attempted to combine these tasks by developing restoration models conditioned on segmentation inputs, such approaches often struggle with complex segmentation errors or inefficient two-stage inference processes. In this paper, we introduce an alternative strategy by integrating a segmentation capability directly into the restoration framework. Specifically, we present a two-way multi-scale generator network capable of both generating high-quality restored images and accurately identifying defects on arbitrary scale regions. This capability is achieved by incorporating a segmentation loss function based on Label-Color Mapping (LCM) into the training procedure. Labels are created by comparing a reference reference image with a degraded input to pinpoint degradation regions, while these regions are represented using multi-scale generators to accommodate variations in size. Without requiring any modifications to existing restoration architectures or additional manual segmentation input, our method enables generators to automatically detect degradation regions during inference. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, proving it superior to current techniques that rely on pre-computed segmentation results to restore images.

The masses and spins of black holes within Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) can be deduced from their electromagnetic spectra due to the fact that their spectral luminosity scales with mass according to the relation $L \propto M$ and with spin as $L \propto a$. This scaling implies that the spectral energy distribution (SED) remains invariant with respect to mass scaling, such that $\text{SED}(M) = \text{SED}(1) M$. This property allows the simultaneous use of multiple mass-independent observables to estimate both black hole mass ($M_{\bullet}$) and spin ($a_{\bullet}$) through the ratio $a_{\bullet}/M_{\bullet}$.

Creating intelligent neuromorphic systems is still difficult, even with significant recent progress. A primary hurdle is the scarcity of accessible, open-source hardware and software, which hinders reproducibility and collaboration. Furthermore, current Neurosystem designs rely heavily on custom, highly specific development environments, making them inflexible and difficult to integrate into broader collaboration workflows. To address these issues, this paper introduces WOOMLE, a versatile, open-source neuromorphic system built on Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ Processing Systems. Designed for hardware/software co-verification and integration into larger research pipelines, it features: (1) a publicly available Python API for real-time monitoring and control; (2) the ability to upload pre-synthesized processor-based hardware accelerators in VWF format; and (3) the capability to run pre-defined simulation stimuli defined in C++ with results exported to CSV. WOOMLE's modular and configurable architecture supports a wide range of algorithms and user-specific applications, demonstrating how an standardized, transparent platform can enhance efficiency, transparency, and collaborative research in the field.

A solar type-I noise storm originates from a microwave burst that exhibits short-duration (less than one second) narrow-band peaks across multiple frequencies. These events typically feature a dual-mode evolution in their spectrograms: a rapid "burst" mode and a more sustained "drifted burst" mode. This study presents the first application of a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to classify these two distinct behaviors in the spectral data of a specific type-I burst. Both the drift rate and the overall duration of the source driving this type-I emission fluctuate over approximately 15 minutes. These parameter variations correlate directly with a microflare event, indicating changes in the height of the flare loop where the radiation originates. Furthermore, the findings suggest a fluctuating connection between the noise storm source and the dynamics of the associated microflare activity.

Abstract: As an indispensable instrument for capturing and cooling free-moving atoms, the magneto-optical trap (MOT) facilitates interactions typically reserved for stationary atoms, such as quantum superposition and coherent control. In our study, we expand the traditional three-dimensional setup to a four-dimensional system using ultra-cold calcium atoms. This advancement adds a degree of freedom through the manipulation of their hyperfine states via an external magnetic field. We further enhance the system's dimensionality by employing three independent, overlapping optical traps within the MOT environment to confine these cold atoms.

We assess the probabilities for (de-)excitation and photon emission involving a non-relativistic neutral atom in motion, interacting with a quantum electromagnetic vacuum in proximity to a perfectly reflecting plane mirror. Our findings extend previous research to a more physical framework, contrasting with an earlier theoretical model that utilized scalar variables for an "electron-" equivalent coupled to a scalar vacuum subject to a boundary on a spacelike hyperplane. Specifically, our calculation of spontaneous emission rates for an initially excited, neutral atom interacting with vector-vector vacuums (electromagnetic fields) reveals a significant influence from transverse motion. As atom-mirror separation decreases, this transverse contribution becomes increasingly prominent. Our results further generalize to include particle exchange phenomena, such as stimulated emission and induced de-excitation, occurring during the atom's movement with boundary interaction.

The ongoing debate regarding whether high-mass stars form in dense pre-cluster environments and subsequently separate, or instead always originate within such clusters, is addressed by this study. By analyzing the Hα emission of 34 O-type stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud using a sample drawn from a specific galactic plane survey region, this research aims to clarify the matter. Evidence for wind-driven stellar emission lines is present in most objects; however, following correction for the background galaxy line, it is determined that 11 O-stars exhibit no remaining line emission. Unlike previously reported stellar candidates with similar spectra—where an O-star identity was sometimes questioned—these 11 stars are confirmed O-stars based on their specific $\lambda$H$\beta$ shapes and flux magnitudes relative to the galactic background. This discovery proves that a significant number of massive stars can exist entirely independent of dense cluster environments, a finding with critical implications for understanding stellar evolution and star formation.

Handwritten documents historically hold significant value across numerous domains; nonetheless, factors such as aging paper, poor storage conditions, and digital scanning artifacts frequently deteriorate the quality of these documents, hindling readability. To address the consequent decline in demands for data entry services manually, this paper introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to restore degraded handwritten document images. This proposed model decomposes the restoration task into two distinct phases: (1) the removal of in-handwriting artifacts (defects, noise, strokes) using instance segmentation to isolate characters effectively, followed by (2) the application of a two-stage autoencoder combined with morphological operations to clean the remaining image issues. A specialized segmentation algorithm tailored for cursive handwriting is integrated into the first phase to achieve precise separation of letters from pen strokes. The second phase utilizes the two-stage autoencoder architecture followed by morphological processing to refocus the model primarily on documents featuring written characters while ignoring swilling motions from the handwriting itself. The methodology is evaluated on two datasets—one collected manually by operators for historical record preservation alongside a newly synthesized cursive dataset. Comparative analyses demonstrate that the model substantially outperforms existing baseline approaches without reaching human performance benchmarks yet, highlighting promising areas for further enhancement.

Evolution in Information Technology enables the exchange of data across devices, demanding ID cards with data easily accessible in machine-readable formats. Consequently, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology is used worldwide to images captured from identification documents to extract this information. This study utilizes Deep Learning for OCR during data extraction from ID cards. Specifically, we apply ResNet-50 to extract and recognize Korean characters from Indonesian National Identity Cards.

Next-Generation Wireless Systems anticipate a surge in Internet of Things (IoT) devices that will depend on vehicular platforms to deliver services. Unlike current research, this study specifically addresses the efficient allocation of non-orthogonal pilot sequences along these future multi-antenna vehicle paths. By formulating a optimization problem that maximizes tracking accuracy across a network of moving vehicles through stochastic optimization and sequence optimization approaches, we provide two specific algorithms: one utilizing stochastic gradient descent and another based on an analytically derived closed-form solution. Simulations confirm that both methods are viable for practical implementation and demonstrate that the proposed sequential pilot strategy significantly enhances overall channel estimation and tracking performance.

We introduce a novel meta-spectral configuration consisting of dual electromagnetic metasurfaces separated by a zero-permittivity dielectric slab. By tuning the electromagnetic metasurfaces, a super-coupling effect arises, enabling the interfaces to emit linear wavefronts that travel simultaneously. This linear wavefront is tunable in inclination, featuring simultaneously enhanced field magnitudes and null phase variation along the entire path. These distinctive line waves offer promising applications for launching linear beams across various orientations and generate singularities, including singularity optics, diffractive spotting, and hidden imaging.

Relation extraction (RE) focuses on identifying the connection between a subject and an object within a sentence. Traditional RE methods often isolate this task from other natural language processing activities, limiting their capability to handle complex sentence structures. This paper introduces a new perspective on RE as a collaborative endeavor involving the joint processing of named entity recognition (NER) and textual semantic matching (TSM). Leveraging this framework, we develop a proposed model, RE-BERT-SEM, which integrates pre-trained language knowledge with external semantic resources. By explicitly modeling the interdependence between identifying entities and understanding their semantic context, our approach enhances RE performance, particularly for challenging tasks like recognizing verbal relations and handling low-frequency relations. Comprehensive evaluations on three standard datasets—RE103, TAC-KB, and RE103s—demonstrate that the model surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques. Specifically, it achieves F-scores of 84.00 on RE103, 73.90 on TAC-KB, and 76.30 on RE103s. Furthermore, ablation studies validate the efficacy of the feature-driven strategy employed.

We investigate the properties of quarkonium states within an N-dimensional space (N-D) that possesses an anisotropic metric. Specifically, we calculate the ground state binding energies and the dissociation temperatures for systems where the medium background varies spatially in an anisotropic manner. Findings from both perturbative and non-perturbative approaches indicate that quarkonium formation is favored in higher-dimensional spaces and exhibits a decreased dissociation temperature when anisotropic effects are present. Notably, while the non-perturbative results in directions perpendicular to the medium are consistently larger than the corresponding perturbative estimates, these values converge as the spatial dimensionality increases.

Traditional covariate shift adaptation methods rely on computing domain-invariant representations or reweighting samples based on their source/target distribution densities. In contrast, this study introduces a novel co-efficient algorithm that integrates adaptation with semi-supervised learning. By leveraging the intrinsic manifold structure of data and performing adaptation through the mutual pseudolabeling process, our approach enhances adaptation effectiveness without demanding pre-computed distribution estimates or complex weight calculation schemes. Experimental validation conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirms the superiority of this proposed method alongside providing crucial insights into the underlying mechanism.

The theoretical underpinnings for why deep learning performs so effectively across diverse tasks remain obscure from a geometric standpoint. This paper visualizes deep learning systems through their analogies to two existing geometries: quantum computation geometry and the geometry used in diffeomorphic template matching. Within this framework, it constructs specific geometric representations for various architectures, including convolutional, residue, recurrent, stacked recurrent neural networks, as well as the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, it examines how these internal geometric configurations relate to model performance at an algorithmic level, suggesting that this geometric perspective could inform the future design of both the architectures and learning algorithms themselves.

This paper introduces a methodological approach to enhance jet substructure tagging using deep neural networks (DNNs) through the integration of expert variables. The strategy involves appending layers containing computed expert variables to the established DNN, aligning their feature representations with both the network's intrinsic outputs and the data-driven characteristics inherent to the architecture. This modification establishes a rigorous framework for incorporating domain expertise, offering simultaneous improvements in model performance and interpretability. Guided by these findings, the authors refine an existing UCB-Z jet tagging algorithm, achieving a notable boost in efficiency: an increase of 15% to 20% in fake rejection at a fixed real acceptance relative to previous results. Relative to other existing taggers applied to the dataset, this enhanced UCB-TAC achieves fake rejection rates comparable to state-of-the-art DNNs while significantly reducing efficiency. Comprehensive analyses support the evidence that expert variables provide substantial benefits in both the accuracy and stability of the model.

This study introduces a newly developed algorithm for the symbolic computation of properties within layer groups, which model systems exhibiting one-dimensional translational symmetry, such as strips and surfaces. The methodology relies entirely on group theoretical principles and utilizes standard open-source software available at no cost. The predicted results apply broadly across various theoretical models defined by their translation-invariant characteristic features within a lattice-defined periodicity. The study emphasizes that the proposed results are applicable to experimental data as input for machine learning algorithms that will be developed in future studies to analyze these phenomena.

Momentum operators acting on intrinsically curved manifolds are identified as Killing vector fields, with their integral curves forming geodesics. A specific class known as isometric circle actions comprises these curvature-related operators; these are proven to occur exclusively on manifolds with uniform negative or zero curvature, which are respectively intrinsically curved negatively or uniformly. Any such circle action corresponds to a geometric structure where the resulting quotient manifold is flat, with the projection serving as a locally trivial principal bundle characterized by this specific curvature relationship. Notably, the absence of curvature variations (curved negatively or uniformly) implies that the underlying manifold must be a model space. The result establishes this defined set of curvature relations as both necessary and sufficient conditions for what mathematicians term a Killing action, where the absence of curvature variations implies a uniform structure.

Deforming the integration contours offers a method to alleviate the sign problem encountered by Monte Carlo simulations away from half-filling. However, the resulting Jacobian determinant within the Boltzmann weight limits generic neural network applications, as their associated computational cost typically scales cubically with volume. By introducing an architecture grounded in complex-valued affine coupling layers instead, we diminish this overhead to linear scaling. The effectiveness of this approach is validated across various system sizes, including one too large to be simulated physically due to the traditional sign problem.

Our composite Higgs framework relies on an $SU(2)_{L}\times U(1)_{X}$ gauge theory featuring global $SO(4)$ symmetry broken to $SU(2)_{R}\times U(1)_{R}$ via a scalar field. This original design included the Higgs composite as part of the scalar sector and incorporated only the weak gauge interaction, hyperforce, gravity, fermion content, and a right-handed $U(1)_{R}$ gauge field. This paper presents an expanded version of the model that integrates the left-handed $SU(2)_{L}$ gauge interaction directly. We examine this extended model under three distinct right-handed $U(1)_{R}$ symmetry scenarios: (i) complete preservation, (ii) discrete $Z_{2}$ symmetry preservation, and (iii) complete breaking to a $Z_{2}$ subgroup. We address the mass generation mechanisms for the W and Z bosons and demonstrate a resolution to the hierarchy problem while ensuring a natural tidal alignment within a sufficiently large, justifiable range. Furthermore, this design offers a plausible origin for dark matter and eliminates unacceptably large contributions to electron electric dipole moments.

"Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations (VPPMs) refer to virtual constructs that either amplify, attenuate, or distort physical stimuli—such as wind, air resistance, or inertia—and modify the magnitude or direction of these stimuli without altering their underlying causes. These VPPMs function to expand the representational frontier for how users interact with and engage virtual environments. Current approaches in haptics and audio rely on traditional feedback modalities, including controllers, haptic surfaces, or visual projections. This paper introduces the novel concept of 'virtual wind,' a new feedback modality that conveys information through physically generated airflow directed at the user. We outline the theoretical underpinnings of this approach, highlight its distinct advantages over existing modalities, and detail the practical hardware required to produce controlled wind.

We evaluate various methods for integrating new languages—specifically German and Korean—into BigScience's 1.3-billion parameter multilingual pre-trained model. This model originally supports 13 languages. The research examines how different factors influence language adaptation performance and assesses the tradeoffs between computational resources and anticipated results.

This research introduces the 'm-ar-CFastICA' algorithm, which integrates the multivariate arabic cross-correlation spectrum method with Independent Component Analysis to enable efficient feature extraction from random signals while minimizing computational complexity. While standard FastICA serves as the foundation for extracting independent components from random datasets, its conventional implementation involves sweepping two-dimensional arrays, resulting in high computational loads. To address this, we replace the multivariate arabic cross-correlation spectrum method, effectively lowering the algorithm's X complexity. Additionally, the proposed method's programming code is developed using the MAT system. Experimental results demonstrate that 'm-ar-CFastICA' successfully achieves modal decomposition across both simulated and actual datasets. Specifically, when analyzing accelerometer signals associated with fault types in rolling elements—such as faults in the outer ring, inner ring, and rolling contacts—the method demonstrates superior diagnostic capabilities. Furthermore, our proposed approach yields signal reconstruction accuracy that equals that of the original FastICA method.

An associated concept to the $n$-fold sum of a ring's additive group is its **cover**, defined as the minimal cardinality of a set whose element-wise sums generate the entire ring; $n$ is referred to as its **covering number**. In advanced "homological theory of rings" studies, computing coverings offers a "combinatorial method to identify the periodic properties of projective resolutions for rings' identity elements." Standard theories suggest that **associative algebras of a fixed cardinality cover with a definite and finite covering number**, yet crucial theoretical queries concerning elements' roles in this measure remain unresolved or under-explored.

Leaning heavily on "combinatorial theory and structural analysis", this paper addresses these theoretical issues. It defines a notion of "associated graphs for algebra elements' roles" to measure element contributions to covering numbers and determines their effects on these numbers.

Social media generates millions of comments and posts about virtually anything. While opinionated text like this makes it hard to fact-check and filter automatically, few solutions exist. In this paper, we introduce a new data-set with over one million real-world, written comments in English about politics in English that are annotated for accuracy. In addition, this paper presents several new benchmarks that are necessary for evaluating the accuracy of natural language checking systems on English written opinions.

Identifying active discussion clusters regarding specific events in real-time social media streams is a critical task, with applications ranging from tracking news stories and detecting hate speech to anticipating emerging crises like the 2020 U.S. presidential election. This study focuses on unsupervised identification of such discussion clusters based on temporal patterns in content and user interactions, offering decisions for automated moderation and review systems. We propose an advanced, fully unsupervised approach that anticipates the initiation of these discussions. By proposing a novel temporal dual-attention mechanism to identify discussions occurring in real time, our method accounts for the importance of individual posts and conversation threads. An attention-weighted sampling strategy is utilized to ensure computational feasibility by focusing on posts from recent timescales, thereby handling user interactions and content temporally. Empirical evaluations on two real-world datasets demonstrate an attentional stream analysis model's superior performance in both computation during and generalization capabilities compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

Building on our previous study which demonstrated that the skew-spectrum offers a robust means of estimating non-Gaussian parameters and probing physics related to dark energy and neutrinos within the non-linear, small-redshift regime of the non-linear matter power spectrum, we advance these methods into the non-linear velocity-space formalism. Utilizing the skew-spectrum derived from the Lagrangian trajectory power spectrum ($P^m_q$) enables independent cross-correlation analysis with the velocity spectrum ($P^v_q$). This approach yields additional constraints on cosmological parameters by capturing non-linear and time-dependent effects that remain invisible in the traditional matter spectrum. Our detailed numerical simulations demonstrate that $P^m_q$ exhibits a strong skew-spectrum signal around $q \sim 5 h\text{Mpc}^{-1}$ arising from the early-time evolution of the velocity field. This internal structure facilitates distinct constraints on the Hubble constant ($H_0$) to a precision of $\delta H_0/H_0 \sim 0.5\%$, surpassing the accuracy achievable via the standard matter power spectrum at comparable scales. Furthermore, substantial overlaps exist in the information content between the skew-spectrum of the matter spectrum and $P^v_q$, reflecting the deep linkage between matter density fluctuations and the velocity field in this high-density, non-linear domain.

By viewing adversarial training within Bayesian learning principles, we introduce a principled framework for optimizing Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) with certifiable robustness guarantees. Utilizing constraint relaxation techniques for non-convex optimization problems, we adapt the popular SOTA BNN optimizer to ensure invariant performance against worst-case perturbations. Furthermore, our approach offers theoretical assurances: under specific conditions, the bounds estimating the upper risk of $ \epsilon $-robustness for the class of $ d $-piecewise constant functions scale logarithmically with the dataset size. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our method matches current SNN algorithms in both accuracy and computational efficiency, while significantly improving the robustness of models against $ l_\\infty $ adversarial attacks—with potential for wider deployment in risk-sensitive applications following further performance tuning.

The proliferation of fake news on the internet has exacerbated the severity of the COVID-19 pandemic, with the surge largely attributed to misinformation regarding preventive measures and treatment. While numerous studies have attempted to identify the propagation mechanisms of such rumors, especially during the outbreak, they often concluded that determining the propagation factors remains difficult due to the intractability of the problem. This difficulty arises from two main sources: first, relevant propagation factor information is missing or obscured during an emergency; second, the structural topology of the internet is dynamic, causing the propagators and propagation pathways to shift continuously. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing that the propagation process itself can be predicted through the integration of multi-source data during the epidemic. The proposed framework, named MWLM, combines denoising autoencoders with multiple-views linear matrix decomposition to clarify the relationship between viral content and viral sources while denewoling associated noise. The results demonstrate that the MWLM approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art systems in classifying the propagators of online rumors during public health crises.

This paper addresses the classification task of hyperspectral images, specifically aiming to reduce the computational cost and memory requirements associated with large datasets containing hundreds of color channels. The study evaluates the effectiveness of three dimensionality reduction techniques—Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and Fisher's Linear Discriminant (FLD)—combined with support vector machines (SVM) and neural networks (NN). Experiments were conducted using publicly available datasets with colors represented in RGB format. Results indicate that while networks generally achieve higher and more consistent classification accuracy than SVMs, these results remain robust across reductions in both the number of color channels and spectral bands. However, it was observed that reducing data volume via compression does not invariably lead to improved pixel classification accuracy. The paper concludes with a summary of classification performance metrics (overall accuracy, average accuracy, and Kappa values) derived from these experiments.

This study introduces ProCS-SP8, an advanced tool for predicting protein backbone amide proton chemical shifts using eight-nearest-neighbor sequences, with models trained against experimental datasets up to 8 neighbors compared to previous limits of only three. The performance improvement in these top-tier models represents a milestone in experimental accuracy, achieving up to 30% greater performance than prior state-of-the-art algorithms at comparable levels of training data by utilizing up to four times more training examples without compromising data quality. The software has been open-sourced for use by researchers around the world. The authors also discuss how the new algorithm can improve structural biology applications including structure determination through NMR and protein engineering. The authors conclude that the new algorithm provides significant improvements over previous methods while maintaining similar overall accuracy on benchmark tests. The authors also discuss the implications for structural biology applications such as de novo structure determination through NMR and other applications. The loss function stands as one of the most critical hyperparameters in a deep neural network (DNN), and for supervised classification, the Cross-Entropy (CE) loss has been the de facto industry standard for over a decade. Driven by the widespread success of models like AlexNet, these networks adopted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)—equivalent to minimizing Cross-Entropy—as their optimization objective, often supported by anecdotal evidence suggesting CE outperforms alternatives like Mean Squared Error. Yet, rigorous comparisons across various losses for other tasks remain scarce. This work presents a comprehensive, large-scale empirical study evaluating multiple loss functions for supervised DNN classification on four extensive and diverse datasets. Utiluing Bayesian optimization to fine-tune every loss function, we demonstrate that, contrary to assumptions, these losses can be equally effective when properly configured for specific classification problems. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of loss functions on model interpretability and calibration, offering guiding principles for future selections of appropriate classification losses.

Investigating collective phenomena demands accurate handling of multi-leg correlations arising from interactions among numerous particles. Parquet theory addresses this by decomposing these correlations into elementary building blocks through specific rules for combination and separation, preserving essential features like screeninge and nested singularities throughout the process. This work details the historical evolution of such correlation rules from their initial formulation until recent developments where a computer algebra system manages the increasingly complex algebra involved.

The phase transition from a semimetal to an excitonic insulator involves pairing electrons and holes due to strong electron-electron interactions. While this effect has been theoretically validated in low-dimensional systems, it has remained unobserved, primarily because achieving such a transition in three dimensions demands exceptional electron density and interaction parameters that were previously thought unattainable. This study reevaluates the feasibility of the semimetal-to-excitonic insulator transition within 3D structures by designing a lattice featuring alternating electron and hole bands separated spatially. Our findings demonstrate that introducing a moderate degree of electron-phonon coupling causes a transition from a standard semimetal to one exhibiting partial PI-symmetry-breaking. Notably, further lowering the electron density or enhancing the coupling strength induces a complete PI-symmetry-breaking, resulting in a true PI-symmetry-state where systems switch to an excitonic insulator. Importantly, this transition can be dynamically controlled by adjusting the electron density or phonon coupling strength. Utilizing this mechanism, we have developed a phonon-mediated, tunable superconducting transition via the excitonic pathway.

Recently, free ride-hailing safety programs have been introduced to allow women and girls to report unsafe situations by enabling them to share their live locations while receiving the comfort of a supportive conversation. The person facilitating this conversation is known as a dispatcher. While traditional training programs prioritize customer service and interpersonal skills, these may not always address the specific emotional and safety-related needs of users feeling vulnerable. Consequently, this research proposes a specialized, emotion-focused training program designed to help dispatchers provide effective emotional guidance and enhance their capacity to support users' emotional well-being. The study evaluates this program's impact through a controlled experiment conducted in Indonesia, comparing it against a standard baseline training. Results indicate that compared to the control group, individuals subjected to the proposed emotion training demonstrated higher success rates in reporting tasks, fewer drops in active session rates, and performed better on post-training assessments regarding emotional handling skills.

This study examines a doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ topological insulator exhibiting spontaneous chiral density wave (CDW) order. By employing a two-band formalism that integrates spin-orbit coupling in topological surfaces states with dedicated CDW order parameters for each spin configuration, we develop the relevant Hamiltonian. Within frameworks of both weak- and strong-coupling regimens, we derive the self-consistent gap equations for the system. Our analysis reveals two stable order phases characterized by right-handed and left-handed chiral states, respectively. We further explore the systematic evolution of these phases as the magnitude of the Fermi momentum ratio between channels varies, alongside examining the influence of doping on the Chiral Anomaly and associated transport phenomena.

Active learning methodologies currently focus on identifying high-value training samples to reduce labeling expenses by exploiting model prediction uncertainty or by identifying data representative of under-exposed regions in feature space. Conversely, data collection in practical applications—such as medical or legal contexts—often results in dense clusters forming cluster boundaries, characterized by sparse intra-cluster regions that possess high value for classification but are rarely selected by labeling selection models despite their significance. To address this, we introduce Cluster Filling Strategy (CFS), a novel active learning framework that targets sparse areas bordering cluster boundaries to identify highly informative samples for labeling effectiveness.

To evaluate shifts in musical styles, I introduce "Loudness Complexity," a metric that analyzes trends within specific audio dimensions over time. By examining roughly 1.1 million songs from the last century using our dataset of over 1 trillion frames from the first 10 seconds of each track (from the "Loudness Complexity" database), I identified several evolving trends. These include changes in the ratio of silence to speech-like sound, overall volume levels, and clarity of musical content. Our analysis reveals a rise in speech-like noise since the 1960s, a gradual increase in loudness through the decades, and more complex and varied loudness patterns recently. These observations align with known stylistic shifts, demonstrating the utility of our approach.

A dominant method for reward learning relies on humans providing preference through comparative pairs, yet this approach demands substantial time as users must scrutinize two action-allocation pairs before determining a preference. To address this inefficiency, we introduce "Once-Thorough-Then-Compare," a model that predicts human preferences even when humans observe only a single action pair per state. Empirical testing on both real-world data synthesized by large language models demonstrates marked improvements over conventional approaches that strictly require paired observations.
