This work investigates a distinct class of singular vorticities in ideal planar fluid flow, merging attributes of point vortices and vortex sheets into what are known as pointed vortex loops. The analysis centers on the coadjoint orbits within the group of area-preserving diffeomorphisms for \(\mathbb{R}^2\) generated by these configurations. It is demonstrated that the corresponding polarization subgroup comprises diffeomorphisms that keep the loop invariant, thereby implying that the resulting configuration space consists solely of loops enclosing a fixed area, with no specific details provided regarding vorticity density or anchor points.

Introducing nAIPW, an extension of the AIPW estimator that accommodates scenarios involving randomization outside of trial data, which also preserves the original AIPW's double robustness while enabling valid inference through standard approaches. A central inference hurdle, addressed by this new estimator, involves the correlation typically found between treatment effect estimators and the randomization information required for their variance calculation, a problem that becomes relevant for researchers utilizing data from clustered trials or per-protocol analytic sets. By employing simulated trial data and demonstrating variance estimation methods compatible with AIPW, we illustrate that the proposed solution yields unbiased treatment effect estimates and precise standard errors.

The ABCD method serves as a robust technique for extracting signal yields and determining properties within experiments that utilize spectral fits or likelihood analyses while accommodating substantial non-signal backgrounds. Although this method inherently introduces a coupling between signal yield parameters and background normalization corrections, this coupling can be effectively decoupled during the subsequent analysis of results. The approach remains particularly advantageous in cases of limited available data. Supporting evidence includes successful applications across multiple analyses at both the ATLAS and CMS experiments, covering scenarios ranging from signal plus background parameter estimation to dark matter search parameters in particle physics.

The different forms of cloud and radiation microphysics are crucial drivers of cyclogenesis within atmospheric circulation models, necessitating that these drivers be validated against both observations and model outputs. Therefore, this study presents a comprehensive evaluation of simulated mid-latitudes cyclone frequencies across four Global Climate Models (GCMs) against actual meteorological data from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). Despite significant discrepancies in the GCMs' resolutions and resolutions and models for the cyclone detection algorithms, we found that the detected cyclone occurrence rates align reasonably well with observations, with a root-mean-square error of approximately 20% and a correlation of around -0.7 on the first principal component. In addition, we demonstrate that the principal components derived from simulated cyclone occurrence rates exhibit significant coherence with those from observational datasets. Finally, we identify that simulated cyclone occurrence rates depend on the specific parametrizations employed for convection dynamics and surface roughness algorithms across the models.

Modelling extreme values is often simplified by utilizing invariant extreme parameter models. These allow a distribution's tail extremes to be characterized effectively without needing domain specification parameters. A study examining the asymptotic distributions of maximum likelihood estimators (MLE) for these parameter models—covering both Type I and Type II—demonstrates the consistency of MLEs for Type I. Additionally, findings from Monte Carlo simulations, which test the accuracy of estimated tail dependence with finite sample sizes, favor Type I behavior. This supports the conclusion that Type I estimated invariant extreme parameter models are superior to their Type II counterparts when analyzing real-world data.

This paper investigates offline reinforcement learning scenarios where an adversary has the ability to modify any fraction $\tau$ of the data within an $K$-armed multi-agent offline Markov decision process (MDA-MDP) environment. Our primary objective is to determine the optimal policy while holding a limited portion of the transition history recorded before offline collection. This paper assumes the availability of the per-decision baseline variance estimator and the access and ability to modify any portion $\tau$ of the data within an $K$-parameter multi-agent offline Markov domain (MDA-MDA) context. This study focuses on online learning capabilities in the absence of real-time exploration. The task involves reconstructing an optimal policy from a modified dataset that may contain arbitrary tampering caused by an adversary, who can modify any fraction $\tau$ of the tuples. The analysis assumes the access to either the user data or a subset of the transition data. The goal is to identify the best possible strategy by minimizing the most significant error sources while only having a subset of the transition data. The overall framework enables the identification of an optimal policy with provable error bounds.

This paper establishes logarithmic convexity as a consequence of an observability estimate at a critical time step for 1-D hyperbolic diffusion systems with dynamic boundary conditions. Our approach begins with a precise derivation of a commutation relation between the associated linear operator and its adjoint, analyzing the resulting properties and implications for the embedded eigenvalues of the discrete spectrum. Leveraging this arithmetic framework, we prove the logarithmic convexity formula and utilize it to derive a local regularity estimate for the heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions within finite difference structures.

Although detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) samples is crucial for the reliability of deep learning models, methods that specifically target coordinate or semantic shifts often fail simultaneously to identify both types. This research investigates the relationship between these two tasks and reveals that every technique previously developed for either task is optimal only for a specific type of shift, leaving a gap where both distributions remain unaddressed by any single approach. To bridge this divide, we present an innovative ensemble strategy named "MetaOOD" tailored to merge the strengths of both classes of methods effectively. Extensive experiments on eight benchmarks demonstrate that MetaOD consistently surpasses all current state-of-the-art solutions in detecting simultaneous coordinate and semantic shifts alongside every existing standalone approach targeting individual tasks.

Recent advancements in single-molecule techniques have facilitated the emergence and investigation of artificial molecular motors, with some designs achieving rotations up to ten orders of magnitude faster than previous iterations using electric currents. Nevertheless, the impact of these currents on motor performance remains poorly understood due to a lack of theoretical framework grounded in kinetic rate theories. This study demonstrates that applying an alternating voltage drives the translocation of a molecular rotor across a gold–molybdenum disulfide–gold junction via such currents. Kinetic analyses reveal that the oscillating electric potential modifies the time-averaged forward and backward reaction rates, thereby inducing net translational or rotational motion in the molecule. Furthermore, theoretical considerations employ a simplified one-dimensional kinetic model to illustrate how these motors can be effectively programmed to execute specific tasks by adjusting experimental parameters like frequency and voltage amplitude.

Origin semantics for transducers were introduced in 2014; since then, numerous characterization and decidability results have contrasted sharply with classical semantics. This paper establishes a further decidability theorem characterizing transducers, specifically near one-way models within origin semantics. It is shown to be possible to decide if a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be made equivalent to a deterministic one-way transducer of origin equivalence through resynchronization by using a bounded regular resynchronizer. This capability stands in striking contrast to standard semantics under non-determinism, where determining if an equivalent one-way system exists is undecidable.

Driven by recent advancements in machine learning and innovative theoretical models, the characterization of exoplanets is accelerating. This study investigates the capabilities of end-to-end spectroscopic retrievals in analyzing extraplanetary systems, leveraging the NGRESS simulator and SPHERES sampler in conjunction with neural network classifiers. Results derived from data generated at 10, 100, and 1,000 nm$^{-1}$ resolution demonstrate that while modeling real-world observational noise poses significant challenges, functional parameters for close-orbiting planets within our own neighborhood can still be reliably estimated. Specifically, analysis of GJ 229B spectra observed by NIRSpec/PRISM on the JWST yields a mean mass of 25$\pm$1 M$_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ (using 100 nm$^{-1}$) and an averaged effective temperature of 450$\pm$10 K. These values align with contemporary spectroscopic estimates for this exoplanet. Furthermore, applying similar techniques to the Proxima Centauri b spectrum, simulated for a planet of 1 M$_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ and 600 K using a 100 nm$^{-1}$ resolution, produces consistent outcomes. This success validates the approach for future applications to more distant exoplanets once observational precision reaches comparable levels to those of the ELT and NIRI instruments.

This research demonstrates within a wide spectrum that no viable triplet state exists below the 2 GeV threshold; thus, such an exotic hadronic state cannot exist within this energy range instead of the expected ground state configuration.

Airborne viruses are carried within suspended droplet nuclei measured in micrometers, expelled by infected individuals through breathing, coughing, or sneezing, and can remain suspended for extended periods. A person contracts the virus by inhaling these particles while they are still airborne or after they settle on surfaces. As the primary route of transmission is inhalation, the concentration of viral particles in the air represents the most significant transmission vector, which is governed by virus generation, air mixing (including ventilation and fan usage), and particle deposition rates. Understanding this distribution is vital for assessing transmission risks. While transmission can occur in both indoor and outdoor environments, indoor settings are characterized by more complex airflow patterns compared to outdoor spaces. Therefore, this study aims to develop a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model to simulate the concentration of airborne SARS-CoV-2 particles inside rooms with varying airflow conditions, accounting for exhalation from multiple infected occupants.

These constraints from $\beta$-decay have subsequently been employed to refine shell-model calculations for more accurate predictions in $np$-shell nuclei.

Current data-driven dynamical systems lack a standard framework for dynamic or experiment design. Existing methods also struggle with high-dimensional modeling due to the sparsity inherent in multivariate dynamics. To address these issues, this paper introduces the Multivariate Autoregressive Networks (MARSNet), a data-driven approach for system identification and control that leverages the concept of a "black system." This conceptual shift enables flexible experimental design and facilitates robust modeling even with sparse multivariate dynamics, offering significant improvements over black-box white-box hybrid methods.

Centuries since its invention, chess has captured global imagination with its simple rules and profound complexity. Despite extensive human analysis, its vast game space continues to challenge comprehensive understanding. By leveraging machine learning, we demonstrate improved insights into opening theory by introducing a novel concept: a relatedness network. Derived from modern chess databases, simple reformulations enable the utilization of widely available graph neural network models. These machines facilitate specific applications, such as refining training plans by suggesting novel repertoires and helping players progress by recommending advanced but accessible openings. Relatedness networks not only deepen our theoretical insight into chess initial moves but also serve as a proof-of-concept for similarly harnessing extensive digital archives in other board games.

We present fresh parameterized algorithms addressing the $k$-outside problem within directed acyclic graphs (DAGs)—specifically, finding an upward planar diagram that minimizes vertices outside the graph. Unlike prior research, our approach handles general outerfaces rather than limiting them to simple cycles. By utilizing a parameter related strictly to the structural complexity of non-bipartite faces, our MIS-cell decomposition enables dynamic-programming strategies for any DAG containing a suitable tree-drawn layout of its associated decomposition tree, as established by this method; this results in our primary contribution to solving the problem effectively when the parameter remains small.

Image-goal navigation presents a significant challenge in artificial intelligence, requiring systems to control an agent moving through environments to locate targets defined by natural language. Although existing research demonstrates impressive results in basic setups, they typically rely on auxiliary information such as pre-existing world maps, environmental dynamics models, or mechanisms for visual state estimation. In contrast, this paper introduces MemoNav, a proposed framework that performs goal-directed navigation using solely environmental pixel pixels, without depending on external maps or dynamics models. This achievement is made possible by two core innovations: Short-Term Memory (STM), which permits the projection of future camera views from current agent states to bridge a gap between the current view and necessary visual representations, and a training curricula strategy for efficient learning. By employing a multi-agent setup where agents dynamically alter their positions within the scene, the method also enables fully decentralized training, ensuring that individual agents retain no knowledge during the process. Evaluation against prior State-of-the-art models demonstrates that the proposed approach surpasses existing methods in both memorization tasks and environments requiring extensive generalization.

To enhance the performance of emerging applications like head-mounted displays and autonomous driving vehicles, traditional cellular networks must complement, not just replace, existing spectrum through additional licensed bandwidth. These new services demand higher data rates achievable via large spectrum allocations (tens to hundreds of MHz) paired with significant network density. This paper investigates the joint scheduling and power control of high-throughput links utilizing such wide bands across diverse time slots, ensuring QoS for both standard narrow-band and wide-band areas while maintaining overall efficiency. First, we formulate a non-convex optimization problem to maximize total cellular sum-rate while satisfying link rate limits and power limits; the solution employs iterative updates based on total rate maximization with successive convex approximation. Next, we present a simplified heuristic for a faster, albeit less optimal, real-world deployment. Simulation results demonstrate that both algorithms perform effectively across various network setups, noting that wider available spectrum allows wider-band links to substantially boost overall cellular capacity.

This study investigates operator growth in systems featuring Lie symmetry. Specifically, the refined entropy spectrum exhibits gaps, with only intermediate levels of information scrambling present, rather than the maximal scrambling seen in generic systems. Ultimately, these findings highlight how Lie symmetry imposes rigorous constraints on quantum information dynamics both within many-body states and during operator evolution.

This study examines the dynamics of inertial brittle fracture in two-dimensional materials, utilizing numerical simulations of dynamic Griffith cracks based on linear elastic fracture mechanics. By analogizing the crack face to slip planes in solids, we observe several key factors influencing crack behavior under high velocity conditions: specifically, an odd-number of steady-state propagation branches, oscillatory instability leading to a transition from a single to triple oscillation, an oscillation amplitude that scales with velocity, and self-similar crack trajectories represented by Fourier series with coefficients dependent on velocity and orientation. These findings suggest that rapid propagation inherently triggers the transition between oscillation modes and the development of complex path features like side branches. Consequently, we conclude that predicting further complexities, including potential mode changes to 5 or 7 branches or additional slip-plane analogies in higher-dimensional materials, requires considering the potential for dimensional reduction inherent in brittle fracture across dimensions 1, 2, and 3.

This paper addresses finite-state channels (FSS) featuring both channel memory and feedback. We establish that the feedback capacity of these systems can be expressed as the spectral radius of a specific matrix defined by the channel's transitions and its underlying probability distribution. Additionally, we analyze an equivalent problem involving finite-state probabilistic transducers (FPTs), demonstrating that the maximum achievable rate of meaningful output information generation corresponds strictly to the transducer's spectral radius. A relevant application of this finding is the theoretical analysis of compression limits in data sequences produced by FPTs when encoding them into a noise-free, single-user communication channel without using side information.

Over-smoothing represents a critical challenge limiting the effective depth of Graph Convolutional Networks. Although existing solutions typically address this by reformulating network architectures or convolutions, new proposals often incur substantial increases in both computational cost and memory usage. This paper presents an alternative strategy to mitigate over-smoothing that requires neither architectural redesigns nor changes to the convolution mechanisms. Instead, our method utilizes an adaptive smoothing coefficient for each sample during training. This coefficient is calculated through a small auxiliary module integrated within the training process but remains absent in the final deployed model. By training this auxiliary component outside of the primary network, the approach avoids the shared representation bottleneck commonly associated with standard fine-tuning, ensuring that both computational and memory requirements remain consistent with those of the standard Graph Convolutional Network.

We report the discovery of seventeen new multiply lensed galaxies in the Proxima Centauri cluster, identified via a blind search within one field of view obtained by the Hubble Space Telescope. This cluster ranks as the most distant proven system for which the Proxima Centauri group has performed extensive gravitational lensing analysis, featuring a rich collection of arc-bearing lenses. Leveraging our prior knowledge of the lens geometry and arc positions, we identified numerous lensed systems that had previously gone unnoticed, significantly updating and expanding our catalog of clusters and arcs managed by the HST Key Project. We evaluated the masses of twelve clusters based on our new datasets and successfully demonstrated that our models, developed through the analysis of multiple arcs and images per cluster, remain consistent with mass estimates derived earlier by the HST Key Project. Furthermore, we utilized strong lensing data from three new systems to place additional constraints on the Hubble constant. Ultimately, integrating the newly discovered arcs and images has not only refined the density parameters of thirteen additional clusters but has also provided robust confirmation that gravitational lensing remains a vital tool for investigating the expansion history of the universe.

The internet's infrastructure is owned by private entities whose primary objective is to maximize profit, which can lead to underinvestment in maintaining network quality. The analysis further highlights that machine learning models offer superior accuracy in estimating COVID-19 impacts compared to conventional statistical regression methods.

X-ray imaging remains a widely adopted method for diagnosing COVID-19, yet its application for predicting disease severity is less explored. These systems aim to forecast the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score using three clinical metrics—COVID-19 diagnosis confirmation, current oxygenation status, and age. Empirical results indicate that the incorporated predefined layers facilitate the automatic derivation of reproducible segment features, enhancing performance beyond standard approaches. Specifically, the proposed framework significantly boosts scoring accuracy when applied as either an SVR or a random forest model, achieving significantly higher accuracy gains as measured by a statistical Wilcoxon signed-rank test ($p < 0.01$).

Socially aware computer vision seeks to comprehend visual events by comprehending their social contexts. This paper introduces "social relationship graphs" (SRGs) as a formalism to represent social contexts, capturing interactions among individuals and their environments. An SRG functions as a graphical model where nodes correspond to people and objects, and edges signify relationships or interactions within the scene. This paper presents SocialR-GN, a novel architecture for generating Social Relationship Graphs from single images. The goal is to learn a latent representation of visual social contexts that GNN can leverage for social event comprehension. Specifically, the model employs an edge generator network that facilitates pairwise interactions between nodes to learn effective representations for both entities and their relationships in the graph. Furthermore, the social event predictor utilizes these graph representations—processed through the combined effects of the graph neural network and relationship prediction modules—to generate accurate predictions regarding social occurrences.

Cascading semantic segmentation represents a recent framework in multi-task learning that addresses the interdependence of prediction tasks through sequential processing. While effective, existing implementations frequently rely on fully connected layers, which often fail to capture spatial structures inherent in computer vision data. To address this limitation, this work introduces a novel solution using dynamic graph message passing (DMPP) networks to explicitly model long-range dependencies within such data. Our proposed Dynamic Graph DMPP network offers a flexible and efficient alternative to traditional fully connected architectures; notably, it contains no fully connected layers and maintains sparse connectivity within the graph. Consequently, this approach not only better preserves the geometric spatial relationships present in image data but also maximizes computational efficiency. The method's efficacy has been verified across multiple scenarios, including non-cell biological cell detection tasks and tasks involving the identification and segmentation within animals, where it significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art models by achieving a marked boost in accuracy.

Optimization strategies such as area scaling and low-area multiplier architectures commonly replace multi-bit multiplication with sequences of smaller operations. This paper introduces a novel algorithmic technique targeting the specific task of computing the product of two 4-bit integers using only three 3-bit partial products rather than multiple multiplications of different sizes. When benchmarked against existing approaches in FPGA environments with varying area configurations across a widely used dataset, this method demonstrated superior efficiency. Our proposed solution delivers a 21.4% average reduction in LUT usage compared to the prevailing state-of-the-art specifically addressing the multiplication of two N-bit integers into 2N-bit results.

We conclude by analyzing potential near-and far-term applications before addressing key obstacles and proposed solutions for the evolution of quantum deep learning.

This work investigates polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTASes) for constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), specifically focusing on cases where a large subset constitutes a unique solution. Driven by interests from diverse fields including molecular biology and personalized recommendation systems, this concept corresponds to robustly approximating CSP problems. Previous research demonstrated that for many CSPs featuring pseudo-boolean constraints, a robust version exists. However, it was established that robust PTASes were unknown for Graph 3-colorability and, more broadly, general q-coloring mechanisms. In this study, we overcome these barriers by defining a general reduction technique that yields a PTAS for $q$-coloring graphs with a constant fraction of robustly unique solutions, provided the problem involves a fixed number of literals per constraint and a constant $q$. We extend our approach to handle multiple variable occurrences, achieving a previous solution for general pseudo-boolean CSPs with multiple repeated variables. Additionally, we analyze a specific previous robust deficit arising from high repetition rates in pseudo-boolean problems and present an enhanced technique generating a robust PTAS by limiting the maximum variable repetitions to $O(\log n / \epsilon^2)$, where $\epsilon$ represents any fixed constant.

Pre-trained transformers have emerged as highly effective models for natural language understanding, yet their internal decision-making processes remain a "black box," posing challenges for interpreting predictions. To mitigate this opacity, we introduce SYNTAX-ATTN, an external algorithm that performs syntactic parsing as a post-processing step by leveraging pretrained language models. Our approach frames syntax as an energy-based syntactically structured system, where query and key linear projection matrices in the self-attention layer function as parameters for these queries. Validity is ensured by a synthetic mechanism that constructs these attention weights based on a defined grammar using a closed-form solution involving only a single sweep of the token sequence. Our methodology is syntactically structured, allowing it to handle both context-free and constraint-satisfier grammatical tasks. Through a top-down parsing mechanism, SYNTAX-ATTN integrates into the entire attention mechanism as part of its post-processing. Our synthesized datasets demonstrate the algorithm's capability in learning syntax and performing syntax-dependent semantic classification tasks. Ultimately, we demonstrate that integrating SYNTAX-ATTN with predictions from foundational transformers can effectively incorporate syntactic patterns into their outputs without incurring additional computational cost during the primary training or inference workflow itself.

This paper continues the exploration of complexity classes defined by regular patterns in a Turing machine's computation history, as initiated in the authors' previous work published in *Theoretical Computer Science*. Specifically, following the methodology outlined in that prior research, we introduce and define a category known as the LIN class, which encompasses decidable languages that admit computations where the yield of every carried operation is directly proportional to the input's magnitude with a constant ratio. Session-based recommendations aim to predict future items by analyzing user behavior patterns within specific time frames. However, these sessions are characterized by being short, sparse, and sparse in item interactions, which significantly hampers traditional recommendation models from learning effective representations and thereby lowers prediction accuracy. Existing state-of-the-state approaches typically focus only on sequential data representations or incorporate both sequential and set characteristics; they struggle to fully capture the unique features of session-based sessions, thereby restricting overall accuracy. To overcome these limitations, we propose Dual Encoding Graph Attention Network (DEGAN), a framework that explicitly models sessions as graphs with two complementary encoders: one for sequence signals and one for set signals. By capturing both data types, DEGAN samples start with two distinct graph views of the session and iteratively refines item embeddings using a dual-path design that integrates sequence encoding signals through message passing enhanced by attention mechanisms aimed at reducing noise. Finally, we employ a loss function leveraging two samples from unsupervised learning principles for deeper feature extraction. Empirical evaluations through extensive experiments demonstrate that DEGAN consistently surpasses current benchmarks in accuracy.

Although recurrent neural networks (RNNs) excel over feedforward architectures in visual object categorization, particularly with cluttered images, the specific function of recurrent information flow in this context remains unclear. This study examines trained object-categorization RNNs with threefold objectives: first, to characterize information flow by measuring representational similarity between layers and between this flow and ground-truth labels; second, to test the hypothesis that recurrence refines object-related signals by correlating stimulus responses with classification performance; and third, to analyze how layer interleaving influences representational similarity. The findings reveal that for simple RNNs, recurrent activity strongly mirrors late feedforward representations, yet this similarity weakens significantly in advanced models, indicating complex recurrent patterns. Furthermore, the correlation between final-layer representations and classification success increases post-training and is substantially higher in RNNs compared to feedforward networks, supporting the view that recurrence fosters classification-relevant features; additionally, representational similarity fluctuates along RNN layers rather than rising monotonically, as predicted by the refinement theory. Lastly, similarity scores generally increase from the first half to the second half of the layer stack, though specific dynamics vary, with visual data compression notably more prevalent in earlier layers than later ones.

Despite significant advancements in non-Hermitian topology regarding free fermions, interactions present numerous challenges. Recently, research into multidimensional Golay complementary arrays (GCA) has been fueled by their promise in omnidirectional precoding for the newly generalized form of Golay complementary matrices (GCM). This study establishes new construction methods for GCA quads and GCA pairs with the help of defined identities across abelian groups, thereby forming GCA quads and GCM quads derived from these findings. This work examines on-shell and off-shell Higgs boson production mechanisms within the context of a strongly interacting decaying state. By leveraging the equivalence representation for longitudinal weak gauge boson scattering and employing a effective field theory for longitudinal components, we construct an amplitude-based model featuring a substantial new physics scale that supersedes the traditional width of the standard model Higgs. Utilizing ATLAS and CMS data regarding the $\gamma\gamma$, $\ZZ$, and $\gg$ channels at 14 TeV, with an accumulated dataset exceeding 36 inverse femtobertaines (inverse fb), and incorporating 2019 CMS data in the $\tt$ channel ($\rightarrow \mu\mu$), we determine parameters defining the Strongly Interacting Higgs resonance by fitting various theoretical frameworks. Our analysis reveals that the Higgs candidate behaves as if it has a width approximately an order of magnitude narrower than its standard model equivalent, with no evidence suggesting it is part of a strong bound state comprising heavy particles such as top partners or vector likeson partners. We also demonstrate that the Strongly Interacting Higgs resonance model provides superior fit quality in the $\tt$ channel compared to standard predictions.

Detecting binary changes in bi-temporal hyperspectral images presents a complex challenge due to the substantial size of the data and the intricate structures that standard techniques often struggle to harness effectively. While recent deep learning approaches have shown promise, they are constrained by the need for extensive supervised datasets—scarce for many real-world scenarios—and a reliance on pre-trained models that demand significant modifications to achieve domain-specific performance. Addressing these limitations, this study introduces a Feature Fusion Deep Convolutional Autoencoder endowed with two distinct sets of convolutional kernels that excel at extracting both spatial configurations and spectral signatures from the input. This architecture supports unsupervised learning by encoding unsupervisedly and decoding with supervisedity for evaluation, thereby eliminating the necessity for large training sets of unchanged samples found in many existing solutions. Furthermore, the methodology relies on the samples present within the bi-temporal pairs themselves for learning, thus avoiding the need for external reference images. Evaluations across three diverse datasets underscore the approach's versatility and effectiveness, particularly in its unsupervised variant which outperforms several current deep learning algorithms.

Optimization is fundamental across many scientific and engineering fields, driving significant efforts from library developers. However, this lack of standardization creates compatibility issues that hinder researchers, particularly in computational physics where memory and floating-point operations must be maximized. To address this, \textit{LibOPT} was created as a unifying framework integrating various specialized solvers with front-end capabilities across multiple programming languages including C++, Fortran, Python, and Julia. Focused on static optimization scenarios, the library supports both continuous and integer variables as well as general convex and strictly convex functions. Currently it features \textit{C++} implementation with provided API wrappers; notably, \textit{LibOpt} encapsulates twenty underlying optimization libraries provided as built-in subroutines.

Natural language processing is a critical academic area focused on comprehending digital text, a process frequently hindered by inadequate digital representations arising from the wide variety of human speech patterns. To evaluate sentence resemblance, two metrics are examined: overlap in sentence overlap distance, and edit distance between sentences .

Spatial anti-aliasing is crucial for both the visual quality and rendering performance of line joins where road segments intersect on vector maps. Given OpenGL's limitations, this task must be handled via off-screen processing using PIL or similar libraries. However, as road counts continue to rise, the computational burden of calculating alpha compositing has become a significant bottleneck. To address this, the current study proposes a spatial anti-aliasing algorithm that employs a GPU-based approach using PIL within OpenGL. By mapping wayshape and road data to textured quads, we leverage two FBOs (Frame Buffers) alongside a pixel shader that performs direct alpha blending based on pixel-layer overlap. This method effectively reduces system load while maintaining high visual fidelity. Empirical tests indicate that our solution is approximately 20% faster than existing solutions, offering superior performance while delivering results indistinguishable from standard anti-aliasing procedures.

This study introduces a streamlined formulation of the radial basis function (RBF) utilizing a hyperbolic tangent function. This hybrid approach unites advantages from both infinite and finite type RBFs while eliminating the convergence issues often limiting infinite variants. When unit radius is assigned, the resulting algorithm converges at an O(n) rate under the unit ball—matching the performance of the compact multiquadric RBF and significantly surpassing the typical conditional O((log n)^n) convergence associated with other infinite variants like Gaussians. Numerical experiments confirm the high accuracy of this modified RBF.

Pulsar halos are a newly proposed source type characterized by a distinct halo of gamma rays surrounding each pulsar. These extended emissions arise when accelerated particles—still within their acceleration timescale—diffuse slowly outward from the pulsar's pulsational residue. Because pulsar halos retain a close link to their central engines, they serve as valuable probes for understanding Cosmic Ray propagation paths throughout the Milky Way. In particular, their ability to smooth out temporal fluctuations in pulsational emissions makes them promising candidates for exploring the high-energy end of the Galactic Cosmic Ray spectrum up to energies of 100 Petaelectronvolts (100 Pev).

We investigate how interest in climate change evolves across various demographic groups and how that attention shifts influences future interest within those same groups. Using data from an English-speaking interest forum spanning the period of 2009–2019, we examine patterns within the US, the EU, and specific European nations while accounting for external events like the Paris Agreement. Our findings reveal that climate change garnered minimal public attention prior to 2010, followed by a surge around 2012–13 that coincided with the Paris Climate Conference in 2 exogenous reference points. Furthermore, we observe that cross-demographic group attention levels are highly correlated, suggesting that changes in attention driven by exogenous events serve as powerful predictors within a network that closely resembles an attention-driven system.

Soft grippers have become increasingly popular due to their compliance, dexterity, and cost-efficiency; yet, achieving precise control remains a significant challenge. Traditional control methods often rely on extensive physical modeling or sensorized components, which compromise accuracy, flexibility, or both. This paper introduces a novel feedback control strategy designed to enhance precision in soft grippers while minimizing the dependency on complex models or sensors. Core to our approach is the use of slow-drifting, linear relationships observed between electrical actuation signals and gripper deformation—a finding validated across various soft materials and geometries. Consequently, our method avoids the need for physics-based modeling while ensuring reliable closed-loop control in practice. We validate the efficacy of our strategy through comprehensive simulations and experimental tests using commercially available off-the-shelf 3D-printed soft fingers. Results demonstrate that this technique improves modeling-based control accuracy by more than 80%, delivering superior positioning performance compared both to open-loop control and various alternative models.

Optimization challenges are fundamental to numerous scientific and engineering fields. Although optimization techniques have existed for over two hundred years and continue to evolve with new innovations, the Gradient Descent (GD) method remains the most prevalent algorithm for addressing smooth nonconvex optimization problems. Despite its popularity, GD suffers from convergence to suboptimal local minima and excessive training times due to its sluggish performance.

This paper proposes an entirely new algorithm termed Lifting Gradient Descent (LGD) for nonconvex optimization problems. By lifting variables to a higher dimension where the objective optimization yields convexity, LGD enables global optimality within an acceptable computational timeframe. Specifically, if the lifted objective is convex, optimizing parameters under certain constraints and applying a backward mapping allows for convergence to a globally optimal solution. Furthermore, to enhance convergence speed, we developed an accelerated version known as MALG (Lifting Gradient Descht Accelerated Method). Both algorithms demonstrate their effectiveness through theoretical proofs of global optimality and numerical experiments. Our experiments highlight that both LGD and MALG converge faster than traditional GD and are capable of avoiding local optima, thereby achieving globally optimal results.

High-redshift radio sources, such as those in AGN jets, young stellar objects, or the core of protogalaxies, offer valuable insights into the evolution of radio-emitting systems. We introduce a novel radio technique to distinguish the evolutionary status of these distant objects, utilizing the geometry of circularly symmetric objects like the L1946 molecular cloud's OH MM1 source or L1457 AL MM2. By applying a statistical test to the OH intensity distribution, we can detect positive deviations from uniformity, as demonstrated by L1457 AL MM2 and L1457 AL MM3. This approach suggests that the L1457 AL MM3 object is a young, compact, and notably symmetric structure. Furthermore, by examining the symmetry characteristics of multiple radio sources, we aim to determine their relative ages, a method validated through the OH MASER group L1457 AL MM3/L1457 AL MM7 example. The findings indicate that the L1457 AL MM3 object is in a more developed state than L1457 AL MM7. Finally, we extend this statistical framework to the high-z NGC430 core, where a uniform distribution test was performed. By analyzing statistical properties, we determined that this region does not contain any compact, symmetric objects.

This study introduces a unified deep learning framework designed for survival analysis in lung cancer, leveraging both textual scan-reported data and multimodal CT images of the lungs. Within this architecture, a multi-label classifier derived from the text data learns survival statuses alongside various lung complications. Concurrently, the module identifies cancerous regions within the visual scans and, crucially, aggregates the features of individual cells to construct representations of the whole organ. Ultimately, these multimodal features are integrated to generate precise survival time estimates. By sharing representation learning components across data types, the model enhances representation quality through multiple task supervision while efficiently handling high-dimensionality and overfitting concerns. Testing on a cohort of 1,000 patients for non-small cell lung cancer demonstrates that this approach significantly improves C-index scores compared to existing baseline models.

Representing states is crucial for learning processes and agents in Reinforcement Learning. In different tasks, this representation is sometimes built from natural language or takes natural language entirely as the input form. This overview analyzes methods found in literature used for constructing natural language state representations. It advocates further for linguistically interpretable and grounded designs, demands careful justifying design decisions alongside the effectiveness evaluation across diverse approaches in both natural language processing and decision-making systems under uncertainty.

We introduce a novel Machine Learning technique (Karl) for extracting cosmological parameters from the full quasar spectra used in gauge analysis. Unlike traditional methods that rely on constructing power spectrum estimators from condensed statistics of quasars, Karl directly inverse a simulated forward model of structure anisotropies to qnasar spectral data. We employ neural networks to learn these simulators, enabling gauge analysis on complete spectral datasets—a capability gauge analysis previously lacked. Using synthetic data derived from the TOMAHAWK hydro simulations, we demonstrate that Karl successfully recovers a power spectrum derived from galaxy simulations with precision, achieving an amplitude accuracy to an amplitude accuracy of 0.02 and an accuracy of 0.02 for its amplitude accuracy. We also assess Karl's performance on gauge analysis with quasars from a high-redshift survey and find that it yields unbiased parameter results with enhanced constraints compared to those from gauge analysis.

This study investigates specific weak modules over Weyl-type Lie algebras, initially focusing on identifying those whose restrictions to the underlying Lie group are irreducible. The authors initially prove a criterion determining when the tensor products of a quasi-finite highest weight module and a "U(h)-free" module remain irreducible. Leveraging this result, they characterize all weak modules that exhibit irreducibility when restricted to the substructure, a approach extended by examining those adorned with a grading. Ultimately, the paper classifies every such weak module resulting in an irreducible restriction to the graded component, specifically addressing semi-simplified graded instances.

Emotional monitoring on platforms like Twitter through sentiment analysis serves companies, as well as private parties; however, the nature of this function has made it increasingly important and challenging, requiring organizations from both sides to keep a close eye. To this effect, this paper includes a diverse of manually labeled, publicly available Twitter datasets, which then go on to showcase an ensemble-based machine-learning approach to this issue.

Open-domain dialogue systems face the challenge of integrating features like topic adherence, user persona, and safety policies due to their complexity and variability across different scenarios. Most current research attempts to enforce these elements via post-hoc monitoring or by distilling human knowledge into large-scale datasets. This work proposes a novel approach that performs joint optimization of policy responses, user modeling, and dialogue generation through a joint training framework. By leveraging large-language model language understanding, a cross-entropy loss function guides the joint training, enabling the system to handle diverse and dynamic policies for both users and hosts without requiring extensive dataset pre-training. Our method simultaneously updates all components end-to-end based on cross-entropy objectives. We validate our approach on the Google Hub's open-dialogue benchmark, demonstrating that it effectively handles difficult conversations, maintains human-like qualities, and satisfies strict, dynamic policies without separate training.

Supersymmetry (SUSY) offers a well-motivated framework for explaining non-observation of neutrinos through a mechanism known as the seesaw, which postulates that right-handed (R-H) neutrinos are extremely heavy. Consequently, this scenario predicts that neutrino mass becomes negligible compared to other sparticles, causing their masses to decouple significantly. We examine the R-H neutral sector during a early universe phase transition that breaks supersymmetry via a first-order transition. Even in the presence of heavy R-H neutrinos, this transition remains second-order (or mixed) in nature and proceeds by converting the Higgs vacuum state by introducing R-H neutrinos and generating a R-H neutrino mass and gravitational wave. The resulting spectrum and decay could potentially lead to a R-H neutrino dominated dark matter scenario. Therefore, this phase transition could also produce detectable stochastic gravitational wave backgrounds from the early universe. The resulting stochastic gravitational wave backgrounds are anticipated that future detectors will soon detect them with high precision.

The concept of machine-generated language inherently carries meaning for both humans and artificial intelligence without necessarily adhering to strict grammatical structures. Leveraging this property of semantic richness within emerging language can serve as a foundation for semantic communication systems. This paper explores how such language can be utilized to facilitate semantic communication between AI agents and humans, effectively bridging the gap in meaning comprehension. By integrating the inherent semantics of machine-generated text, these systems enable more intuitive interactions, moving beyond traditional engineering constraints to align with the fundamental principles of semantic information transfer. Ultimately, this approach fosters the development of efficient semantic communication networks that accurately convey meaning across different cognitive domains, including human-computer and inter-machine communication.

A fundamental challenge in Natural Language Processing involves word prediction, where a sequence of words is presented with a single gap for the model to fill. This paper explores the visual aspects pertinent both to exploratory data analysis and the design of interpretive diagrams for interpretive machine learning models. Through techniques such as word frequency analysis and various visual representations, the visual features useful for understanding how interpretive machine learning models work and creasing insights into how they might be improved are identified.

Recent progress in session-based recommendations has attracted significant interest into contextualized sessions and cross-session prediction methods. However, existing context-based prediction models struggle with capturing long-term user preferences, whereas cross-session techniques fail by ignoring the immediate context of individual user interactions. To address these limitations, this paper proposes the **Spatio-Temporal Context-based Network (STC-Net)**, a deep learning framework designed to simultaneously leverage the sequential dynamics within sessions and the predictive signals between them, thereby capturing user behaviors more effectively at both granular and macro scales. Furthermore, a novel sequential dual-stacking architecture integrates both session and cross-session predictions through a hierarchical multi-task approach. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that STC-Net consistently surpasses state-of-the-art baselines, delivering superior recommendation accuracy.

We investigate dimers composed of two passive colloidal spheres connected by a reversible, passive adhesive bond that responds passively to local conditions. When placed in a bath of active particles which self-propel until they deplete fuel, gradients of activity induce passive dimers to migrate toward either high or low regions of activity, depending on observation scales. Specifically, at large length scales, these aggregates behave passively, moving up activity gradients, whereas at small length scales, they exhibit active motion moving down activity gradients. This transition between upward and downward mobility is governed by activity-induced fluctuations in bond length balanced by chemical potential drives, while on mesoscopic scales a striking phase separation can occur where clusters move alongside solitary active particles coexisting with a down-walking component.

We introduce a robust method based on the Generalized Finite Element Method (GFEM) for efficiently modeling single-phase flow in fractured porous media. Unlike the discrete fracture network (DFN) approach used by many GFEMs that discretize every fracture across the domain, our model represents each fracture with a single degree of freedom, defining interface values on the fracture centerline. Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion (TKGC) has emerged as a popular technique for reasoning about event and temporal data graphs, specifically aimed at inferring missing information using rule-free methods. Within this area, TKGC can be categorized into two primary classes: two-step and end-to-end systems. In contrast, end-to-end systems directly process text without preliminary extraction steps. This survey provides a structured overview of the current research landscape by first categorizing end-to-end text-based approaches before two-step systems. Furthermore, the study evaluates various text-based methods from an end-to-end perspective along the feature engineering, model design, and training strategies. Furthermore, the characteristics of effective contextual texts are explored. While rigid-body impact synthesis methods often generate accurate audio samples of grounded surfaces, whether this audio remains perceptually discernible when such sounds are used RTOY modelically within a simulation depends on various elements. These factors encompass the characteristics of the colliding bodies (such as mass, stiffness, velocity, and acceleration), the specific impact configuration, and the acoustic coupling between the ground and the listener. Previous attempts at controlling virtual ground adaptation adjustment have been limited because they relied primarily on a single metric: the magnitude of impulse transferred from impact to ground without addressing other critical variables. This paper introduces an enhanced model that quantifies perceptual detectability as a composite function of impulsive force characteristics, modal matches, and coupling metrics. We outline individual sub-contribution functions for each factor, each supported by a function governing their relevant parameters. Each component is calibrated against measured coupling values and modal alignment values using listeners for threshold detection and impulse patterns for identifying detectable impacts between two objects across varying distances. The standard demonstration of quantum entanglement without invoking inequalities, exemplified by the "all-versus-nothing" proof of Bell nonlocality, bifurcates into two categories: the "always" variant, which asserts entanglement for every state within a specific set, and the "sometimes" variant, which affirms it only for certain realizations from certain entangled state families. Prior research predominantly relied on assumptions that restricted the construction of such proofs to only perfect correlations. Consequently, this limitation necessitated the reliance on "sometimes-type" proofs for general nonlocal or multipartite entangled states, permitting only partial correlation patterns. This constraint is herein eliminated. We introduce a flexible framework capable of establishing "always-type" proofs for any demonstrated nonlocal state, irrespective of how many measurement settings each observer employs or the specificity required to observe effects, including cases previously thought unprovable via "always" logic for general states with finite measurement configurations.

Traditional clustering focuses on grouping similar dynamic systems based solely on their current, time-invariant states. Numerical relativity simulations involving non-trivial matter configurations require solving the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints alongside the evolution equations. We present an innovative method to enforce the Hamiltonian constraint within the "1+1+1" numerical relativity framework using Godunov-type finite difference finite volume techniques. This approach employs a flux-splitting strategy on fluxes derived from the gradient of metric scalar density, necessitating no assumptions about numerical discontinuities in those gradients. Consequently, this method is robust for handling shocks and general discontinuities within matter or fields, although it proves less efficient for smooth shock-free scenarios. It can function either independently as a standalone solver or be integrated as a fully coupled predictor-corrector algorithm to integrate Einstein's field equations directly. Initial assessment of this new scheme is performed via 1+1 numerical relativity models featuring static and collapsing dust shock tubes.

Long sequence time-series forecasting plays a vital role across numerous applications, including power grid management, network traffic prediction, and demand analysis. Pre-trained language models have emerged as vital components of recent ranking systems, yielding remarkable performance. Knowledge distillation serves as the key strategy to sustain such high performance with efficient computation. Our work centers on two fundamental problems in creating knowledge distillations for ranking: effectively aggregating information from multiple teachers and incorporating label information throughout the distillation process. Addressing these challenges simultaneously with a unified approach called Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), which iteratively ensembles logits from various teachers under label supervision, has proven successful. Our experiments, covering both offline and online settings, show competitive outcomes, and this method is now live in a commercial search system.

Ultralight bosonic dark matter (BSDM), predicted to exist in quantities large enough to interact with nuclear-scale systems through quantum effects. Under these conditions, BSDM appears as an ultralight bosonic field with oscillating number density, inducing time-varying, spin-independent forces that push on free-falling masses. Because these accelerations generate minimal relativistic time-dilation, the resulting frequency shifts are nearly negligible. However, the acceleration is nearly constant in the laboratory, producing significant frequency components at low frequencies. Upto certain limits, these low-frequency signals are more strong and thus easier detect than faster varying, high-frequency components. Consequently, we can use existing or near-future low-frequency detectors to search for these signals. The chosen dark matter masses are such that the field varies slowly within our lab frame, allowing the oscillating density to exert a almost constant push on free-falling objects. Since acceleration terms dominate at low frequencies (due to the derivative properties), we can detect these ultralight signals using sensitive accelerometers, gravity gradiometers, or geophysical detectors that monitor tiny differences in freefall for different objects.

This research investigates a one-parameter family of linear operator equations characterized by a radon measure support in the domain $[0,1]$. While the left-hand side features the measure associated with Rademacher random variables, the right-hand side represents low-frequency Fourier coefficients. Our primary objective is to delineate a sufficient condition ensuring the existence of a unique solution within the space of radon measures for each right-hand side input. Under this non-degeneracy framework, the work analyzes the stability properties of the solution map along with the minimization of the corresponding regression risk. Notably, the authors establish that, given an appropriate choice of regularization parameter, the proposed linear problem serves as an effective method for recovering the measure $\mu$. Specifically, the risk bounds derived for this linear approach coincide in form with those achieved by the widely used Lasso estimator.

The P4 language has emerged as a prominent, programmable interface for developing custom implementations of network layer 4 (L4) devices known as P4 switches. Although capable of precise and exact matching to filter packets based on specific fields, achieving fine-grained control over forwarding behaviors—such as modifying packet headers or controlling output queues—often necessitates additional mechanisms. These traditionally include specialized extensions, complex control programs, or embedded Turing complete logic, all of which raise concerns regarding system reliability and security. This paper introduces a data plane-centric approach to crafting program-logic for P4 processors, specifically avoiding the need for explicit state management. Furthermore, it outlines corresponding compiling strategies to facilitate complex data transformations and interaction with quality-of-queue (QoS) features. Most significantly, it demonstrates this plan, allowing systems to be deployed directly on hardware with minimal or no involvement of underlying states by the program developers and operators themselves.

The resulting scheme is presented within an explicit time-stepping fluid framework, demonstrating second-time-order and third- spatial-order consistency. Temporally refining the transport solves enables convergence rates to leap from the expected (hence, spatial) third-order toward higher efficiencies. This suggests significant improvements in both accuracy and efficiency by adapting time integration steps and associated transport resolutions.

This new method class has interesting properties related to continuous-stage Runge-Kutta techniques that were revisited here for a broader range of general derivatives problems.

We introduce a novel multi-scale gradient signal that guides the automatic determination of optimal depths during neural network training, allowing for dynamic layer group adjustments with only marginal increases in computational cost compared to standard backpropagation. The approach employs two auxiliary networks termed "critics," positioned either before or following each group, that estimate a value for every individual layer relative to that group. These internal estimates are then contrasted against a global assessment of each group's value computed by a network spanning the entire model. As total output derivatives propagate backward through the full architecture, the multi-scale signals derived from comparing internal and group-level values automatically modify how learning rates are distributed within each group. Consequently, the frequency of parameter updates for that group is regulated based on its task significance. The value assessments provided by these local critics determine an adaptive learning weight, ensuring groups receive more frequent updates when their contribution to the overall objective is greater, while a unified signal governs all parameters. We demonstrate this technique on the Graph Attention Networks (GATMs) structure applied to molecular property prediction, showing it refines the allocation of learning rates to better align with downstream tasks and significantly boosts performance when combined with standard global optimization strategies.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering flows in three-dimensional chaotic scattering flows in three-dimensional open Hamiltonian systems are studied here. Three prototypical systems forming tori with interpenetrating tori and double tori configurations across parameter ranges exhibiting chaotic scattering are examined. In undamped systems, non-Wada basins appear, but all such examples transform to becoming surrounded by chaotic sea when even minimal damping applies across prototypical systems. However, adding friction creates a dissipative attractor where a single basin is found. We observe that weak dissipation shifts bifurcation thresholds to higher values relative to the conservative counterpart, while the magnitude of the applied friction alters scattering time and count significantly. Ultimately, strong friction induces point vortex behavior.

Recognizing human activities in unposed video clips is a highly investigated computer vision challenge. While many models represent video as ordered frames or feature blocks to capture temporal relationships, these linear assumptions often overlook complex and irregular directional structures found in dynamic feature spatial-temporal patterns. To address this limitation, this study introduces Hierarchical Attention Networks (HAN), a novel deep learning architecture that explicitly decodes these structures within blocks of form, space, and time. Instead of adopting a sequential view, HAN treats each block as anchored in its absolute temporal position alongside other relative temporal offsets, creating directional dependencies via sequential modules anchored at these unique markers. Furthermore, the model integrates form- and space-level attention to pinpoint discriminative visual elements across camera angles and enhances learning by aggregating form and spatial dependencies into the temporal layer. Experimental results show HAN significantly surpasses current top performers in accuracy for unscheduled action detection, all while utilizing significantly fewer parameters and accelerating training and inference speeds.

This piece provides a brief overview of the principles surrounding star formation and its evolution based on observational evidence, showing that it is particularly meaningful in this light as the creation of planets is simply a side effect of stellar processes. Consequently, the entire inquiry regarding life throughout the universe and its origins can be approached from an innovative standpoint.

This study develops a class of probability distributions defined by three parameters, intended as a flexible alternative to existing family. Its flexibility is demonstrated through maximum likelihood parameter estimation, showing these parameters can capture significant features from probability distributions related to the COVID-19 pandemic within specific regions. Additionally, Shannon entropy and mutual information calculations are employed to analyze random and shared information levels among the distribution's parameters based on COVID-19 data sets.

We examine a modeling framework for semiconductor manufacturing, where wafer throughput and deposition thickness are governed by a coupled system of a scalar conservation law and an ordinary differential equation (ODE), the latter contingent on flow conditions within the transport equation. This system exhibits discontinuous transport speeds stemming from its intrinsic structure, necessating the utilization of an entropy-mixed solution concept and a corresponding numerical upwind scheme. We establish the convergence of this scheme, demonstrating that the limits satisfies the formulated entropy-mixed solutions. Furthermore, our computational analysis investigates discrepancies in speed discontinuities and their impact on estimating wafer throughput and thickness analytics.

Cybersecurity threats pose significant risks to organizations worldwide, where even minor breaches can cause substantial financial losses and damage a company's reputation. Detecting these breaches promptly is therefore essential to mitigate harm. While traditional intrusion detection systems rely on statistical features extracted from network traffic, the rise in the volume and velocity of data has intensified the workload on existing computational resources and specialized algorithms to identify threats efficiently. This study introduces a novel approach utilizing Deep Learning for intrusion detection via TCP-based network traffic analysis. Furthermore, it uses the randomly forest technique as a mechanism to optimize the Deep Learning model. Experimental evaluations indicate superior accuracy compared to state-of-the-art alternatives.

This paper demonstrates that for any countable discrete infinite amenable group admitting a Schreier growth gap, there exists an associated free probabilistic structure consisting of free pseudo-groups and free $*$-$$C^{*}$-algebras.

Animals move to navigate complex challenges such as foraging, escaping predators, and exploring new territories. Despite this multifaceted nature, locomotion is frequently engineered as a simple forward translation in both biological research and education. This paper introduces a new paper-based model of a snake that challenges these limitations. Developed through collaboration between engineers and biologists, this system utilizes advanced fabrication techniques to create highly realistic actuated models. General feedback indicates users benefit from interactive exercises and problem-solving tasks that involve designing solutions snake-specific constraints. These activities effectively teach the importance of bioinspired animals, highlighting a niche for further research and application in both locomotion and snake manipulation contexts.

Optimizing excess electricity stands as a vital component for power transmission networks aiming to cut expenses and enhance the efficient utility of available current. This paper demonstrates the application of quantum annealing techniques to an integer programming Dantzig-Glover formulation designed specifically for two-node bid networks. By systematically varying instances, we evaluate performance across both a real-world standard test system and various randomly generated scenarios. Our analysis compares outcomes from the Dantzig-Glover approach against a simplified model featuring both alternating and direct flows, ultimately evaluating the resulting solutions using accessible quantum annealers.

Current machine learning and AI techniques predominantly extract rules from datasets that serve as historical records of measurements, yet deriving universal physical laws from such data alone is challenging. This difficulty stems from two main issues: the data does not explicitly reveal the equations governing the phenomena, and it may contain noise that hinders accurate inference. Although AI and ML models can successfully learn the probability distributions underlying these measurements, such models do not themselves constitute physical laws. Consequently, there is a critical need to bridge the distinction between these data-driven models and true physical laws, a change of paradigm often referred to as the "Data-to-Law" problem.

This paper introduces a conceptual framework wherein a "Data-to-Law" model serves as an intermediate step between traditional machine learning and explicit physical laws. This intermediate structure possesses characteristics shared by both the other paradigms, with specific focus on Bayesian ordinary differential equations (BODEs). BODEs function effectively for inferring dynamics from noisy observations and accommodate prior knowledge. A demonstrated application of BODEs tracks the evolution of a quantum many-body system's wave function using matrix product states as a representation.

This work details a search conducted by the ATLAS detector at the LHC for hypothetical heavy, electrically charged particles with long lifetimes that decay into final states containing b-jets within two distinct regions characterized by low background levels and high purity. These regions were chosen specifically due to their high purity. It presents a comprehensive theoretical framework involving charged massive long-lived particles and their specific interactions leading to b-baryon rich hadronic jets under electric and magnetic fields. To analyze these phenomena, we specifically focus on Upsilon mesons within the hadronic jet spectrum and evaluate the meson's contributions using the Bethe-Heitler model for nuclear radiation. The analysis ultimately establishes 95% confidence level statistical limits on particle masses across a wide spectrum of lifetimes. Based on this analysis we can set new limits on the mass of the given charged particle in air-core fiber detectors with varying dimensions and densities.

Creating reliable single-photon sources is essential for practical quantum information processing, with radiation from isolated confined particles like atoms or molecules among the most proven methods to generate these photons. However, these traditional approaches often struggle with low emission efficiency due to photons being lost into radiation modes that cannot be captured easily. This study presents a quantum efficiency measurement of a standardized atom-based single-photon source using photon Bayesian inference to address such uncertainties. The results reveal a high quantum efficiency of 0.81 ± 0.02 when paired with an efficient single-photon detector. Furthermore, we demonstrate a maximum Purcell factor of 77.5 ± 7.7 for a source yielding a third-order coherence value of $g^{(2)}(0) = 0.0012 \pm 0.0002$, largely overcoming losses previously attributed to inefficient detection systems.

Contemporary experimental data demands high precision predictions for particle colliders; as theoretical precision rises, calculating complex quantum corrections—specifically, fully differential three-loop electroweak and mixed electro-weak-QCD terms—involves significant difficulty. Obstacles include intricate integrand topology with numerous legs, intricate propagator structures, numerous numerical scales, intricate multi-scale integration patterns, multi-loop integral reductions, integrations across multiple phases, parametric integrations, and numerical evaluation. This paper presents strategies to resolve these difficulties within the context of three-loop corrections featuring multiple bosonic contributions. Key approaches utilized are multivariate partial fractioning to reorganize exponentials from bosonic loops, facilitating the reduction of their parametric integrals, combined with a comprehensive numerical integration framework tailored for such complex computations. Finally, the paper demonstrates these methodologies by calculating the totally radiated, totally charged vector boson correction spectrum for top-quark pair production via the $pp \to tt\ell\nu$ process.

In systems with random scattering, a deposition matrix $W$ connects the matrix of measured transmissions $T$ to the system's internal scattering matrix $S$ via the relationship $W = T \cdot S$. While $T$ is readily obtainable from experiments, $W$ can subsequently be analyzed using models—such as those based on wavefront jigsaw theory—to derive the distribution of scattering sample strengths ($p|g|$). This paper reports the results of a study involving the analysis of two-dimensional systems with microsphere inserts to determine the distribution $p|g|$ of scattering sample strengths. Furthermore, various methods for resolving the ambiguity arising from the equivalence between different pairs $(T, S)$ and $W$ are examined by applying a dispersent-scattering model. These approaches utilize the diagonal elements of the matrix $W$, specifically its trace, to generate distributions that originate from unambiguous $(T, S)$ pairs.

The two-arm structure of the Galaxy, comprising its Far Arm and Near Arm, serves as a critical component of our understanding of the Galaxy's central geometry. Although these arms generally diverge in position, they converge and effectively merge within a distance of $5$ kpc from the center, necessitating high-precision stellar kinematic data to map this inner region accurately. Utilizing data from the Gaia EDR3 release, we have generated a new mask to identify stars belonging to the Galaxy's nucleus and the inner segments of both the Far and Near Arms. Our analysis demonstrates that beyond a galactocentric radius of approximately $4.5$ kpc, the two structures merge. Furthermore, we identified a remarkable symmetry in the distribution and kinematic properties of both arms within the outer regions (beyond approximately 15 kpc from the galactic center), whereas significant structural and kinetic differences persist in their shared proximity to the core ($\leq4.5$ kpc). Additionally, we observed clear rotational asymmetries characteristic of a non-circular rotation pattern typical of spiral arms; however, these effects are markedly more intense in the inner regions where both structures meet compared to their positions at larger distances.

The growing application of optimization methods has led to an increased focus on diverse groups of solutions. Consequently, variety independence measures have been proposed to identify and foster solution diversity across various domains, though no single metric universally captures the needs of every problem. Quasispecies, a concept from molecular evolution, offers a promising framework for understanding diversity within populations, yet its computational complexity has previously limited its practical application. This work introduces a computationally efficient approximation of the measure for use in optimization, which was tested and validated against high-dimensionality functions alongside various evolution strategies. The findings highlight that integrating a quasi-similarity metric into the search process successfully discovers regions of the landscape that strategies typically avoid, filling gaps otherwise difficult to reach. Most significantly, results demonstrate that generating a collection of distinct solutions via quantity diversity significantly surpasses the optimization success rates traditionally used alone.

The concept of Matching with Three Pairs extends the traditional Stable Roommates problem to settings involving groups of three participants each. Recently, this model was explored by Manlove et al., who demonstrated that even with the addition of stability as a core criterion, finding a solution becomes NP-complete. Building on this foundation, the current study investigates a collaborative variation where participants are grouped into triads using preference lists, stability rules, and symmetric valuation methods. While this specific configuration allows for a polynomial-time resolution, the research establishes a critical finding: identifying symmetric triads within the dataset is NP-complete. Consequently, establishing a fully stable matching remains computationally intractable. To address these challenges, the authors present a dedicated algorithm designed to locate stable triads efficiently, even when full stability proofs may elude participants due to computational complexity.
